title: Forces change shape, speed and direction

summary.text: Press a ball of dough and it stays flat. Squeeze a sponge and it springs back. Press a biscuit and it breaks. A force is a push or a pull. It can change a thing's shape by squashing, stretching, twisting or bending it. Forces also start, stop, speed up, slow down and turn moving things. A bouncing ball is squashed for a moment, too fast to see. Even a steel table changes shape a tiny bit when you press it. Pushes and pulls also shape your bones, trees and the Himalayas.
summary.art: A ring of pictures around one child's hands: dough squashed flat, a rubber band stretched, a wet towel twisted, a bamboo bent, a cricket ball squashed against a bat, and the Himalayas folded like a crumpled cloth.

intro.hook: Press your thumb on a table. Did the table change shape? You can't see any change. But it did bend, a tiny bit. Scientists can show it by bouncing a laser beam off a mirror lying on the table.
intro.text: Get a ball of chapati dough. Squash it, stretch it, twist it and bend it. Each push or pull changes its shape, and the new shape stays. Now squeeze a sponge and let go. It springs back. Now press a biscuit. It cracks. The same push did three different things. In this unit you find out why, and how even hard things change shape when they are pushed.
intro.art: A child's hands on a kitchen counter, with a squashed ball of dough, a squeezed sponge springing back, and a cracked biscuit side by side.

outcomes: I can say that a force can change a thing's shape, and show four ways: squashing, stretching, twisting and bending.
I can sort things by what they do after a force: keep the new shape, spring back, or break.
I can run a fair test, like dropping clay from different heights, measure the change, and show it in a table and a bar chart.
I can explain that a bend is a squash on one side and a stretch on the other, and that folds and tubes make things stronger.
I can say that forces also start, stop, speed up, slow down and turn moving things, and that a bounce changes both shape and direction.
I can give examples of forces changing living things and the Earth: bones, trees, the Himalayas and the spinning Earth.
I can explain that shapes change because atoms are pushed closer or pulled apart, and say what scientists still do not know.

terms.meaning: A push or a pull. Forces can start or stop things, speed them up, slow them down, turn them, or change their shape.
terms.example: You push dough flat with a rolling pin. You pull a rubber band longer.
terms.art: Two arrows: a hand pushing a rolling pin over dough, and two fingers pulling a rubber band.

terms.meaning: The outline of a thing, and how it fills space. Round, flat, long and curved are all shapes.
terms.example: A ball of dough is round. A rolled chapati is flat.
terms.art: A round dough ball next to a flat chapati.

terms.meaning: To push on something so it gets flatter or smaller. Scientists also call this compressing.
terms.example: Sitting on a cushion squashes it. Stamping on a can squashes it.
terms.art: A child sitting on a cushion, the cushion pressed flat.

terms.meaning: To pull on something so it gets longer or thinner.
terms.example: Pulling a rubber band. Pulling chewing gum. Pulling a piece of dough into a long snake.
terms.art: Two hands pulling a long rubber band.

terms.meaning: To turn one end of something one way while the other end turns the other way, or stays still.
terms.example: Wringing water out of a wet towel. Twisting a snake of dough like a rope.
terms.art: Two fists wringing a wet towel, drops falling.

terms.meaning: To make something curve. A bend squashes one side and stretches the other side at the same time.
terms.example: A bamboo pole bends in the wind. A ruler bends when you press its middle.
terms.art: A bamboo bending in the wind, the inside curve and the outside curve marked.

terms.meaning: What a thing is made of.
terms.example: Wood, steel, rubber, clay, glass and cotton are materials.
terms.art: A row of small pieces: wood, steel, rubber, clay, glass, cotton.

terms.meaning: Springs back to its old shape when the force stops.
terms.example: A sponge, a rubber band and a tennis ball are elastic.
terms.art: A sponge squeezed in a hand, then the same sponge back to its shape.

terms.meaning: When a thing keeps its new shape after the force stops. In science, 'plastic' means 'stays changed'. It is not the stuff bottles are made of.
terms.example: Clay, chapati dough and a bent paper clip keep their new shapes.
terms.art: A thumbprint pressed into clay, still there after the thumb lifts.

terms.meaning: Breaks or cracks instead of bending much.
terms.example: A biscuit, a papad and glass are brittle.
terms.art: A papad snapping into pieces.

terms.meaning: A thin split in a thing. Brittle things break when a crack runs all the way across.
terms.example: A cracked tile. A cracked eggshell.
terms.art: A tile with a thin crack running across it.

terms.meaning: A test where you change only one thing and keep everything else the same. Then you know what made the difference.
terms.example: Drop the same clay ball from different heights. Change only the height.
terms.art: Two identical clay balls, one held higher than the other, with a tick beside 'only the height changes'.

terms.meaning: How fast something moves. Something with more speed goes further in the same time.
terms.example: A bowled cricket ball has more speed than a rolled marble.
terms.art: A fast cricket ball with long speed lines next to a slow marble with short ones.

terms.meaning: The way something is moving or facing, like left, right, up or down.
terms.example: A batsman sends the ball back the other way. That changes its direction.
terms.art: A cricket ball's path arriving at a bat and leaving in a new direction, shown with arrows.

terms.meaning: How much matter is in a thing. Matter is what all things are made of. The more mass a thing has, the harder it is to start, stop or turn.
terms.example: A full school bag has more mass than an empty one. It is harder to swing round, and harder to stop.
terms.art: Two school bags hanging from hooks, one empty and floppy, one full and bulging.

terms.meaning: When a moving thing hits something, squashes for a moment, then springs back and moves away.
terms.example: A tennis ball hitting the floor squashes a little flatter for a moment, then jumps back up.
terms.art: A tennis ball squashed flat against the floor, with an arrow going down and another going up.

terms.meaning: A sharp bend pressed into a sheet. Folds can make a thin sheet much stiffer.
terms.example: A paper fan. A wavy tin roof sheet. The wavy middle layer of a cardboard box.
terms.art: A sheet of paper folded into a zigzag fan, holding up a small book.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block that everything is made of. Atoms are far too small to see, even with an ordinary microscope.
terms.example: Clay, steel, your bones and the air are all made of atoms.
terms.art: A zoom from a steel spoon to a speck to a grid of tiny balls.

terms.meaning: The hold between two atoms. It acts a little like a tiny spring. Push the atoms closer and it pushes back. Pull them apart and it pulls back.
terms.example: When you bend a steel spoon a little, you are pulling and pushing on more of these tiny holds than anyone could count.
terms.art: Little balls joined by tiny springs, some squashed and some stretched.

terms.meaning: The hard, living parts inside your body that hold you up. Bones are alive, and they slowly change shape to match the pushes and pulls on them.
terms.example: The bones in a tennis player's playing arm grow thicker than in the other arm.
terms.art: Two arm bones side by side, the playing-arm bone a little thicker.

terms.meaning: A giant slab of the Earth's rocky outer layer. The plates move very slowly, about as fast as your fingernails grow.
terms.example: India sits on a plate that is slowly pushing into Asia. That push built the Himalayas.
terms.art: A map of India as a slab pushing north into Asia, with the Himalayas crumpled up where they meet.

terms.meaning: A ripple in space itself. As it passes, it stretches and squashes space by a tiny amount.
terms.example: In 2015, scientists measured a gravitational wave from two black holes crashing together far away.
terms.art: A grid like a fishing net, rippling, with two dark balls spiralling together in the middle.

explanations.definition: A force can change a thing's shape. There are four main ways: squashing, stretching, twisting and bending.
explanations.description: When you push or pull something, it does not just move. It also changes shape, at least a little. Pushing inwards squashes it. Pulling outwards stretches it. Turning its two ends opposite ways twists it. Pushing on its middle while its ends are held bends it. Often one action does two at once. Rolling a chapati with a rolling pin squashes the dough and stretches it wider.
examples: Squash: pressing a ball of chapati dough flat.
Stretch: pulling a rubber band, or chewing gum.
Twist: wringing out a wet towel, or twisting a strip of dough into a rope.
Bend: a bamboo in the wind, or a ruler pressed in the middle.
explanations.art: Four panels of the same dough ball: squashed, stretched into a snake, twisted like a rope, bent into a horseshoe.
explanations.context: This card explains the main idea of the unit: forces can change shape, in four main ways.

explanations.concept: Keep it, spring back, or break
explanations.definition: After a force stops, some things keep their new shape. Scientists call this a plastic change. Some spring back to their old shape. These are elastic. Some crack and break. These are brittle.
explanations.description: Clay and dough stay squashed, so they are good for making pots and chapatis. Sponges, rubber bands and balls spring back. A biscuit, a papad or glass cracks instead. The same thing can do all three. Bend a steel paper clip a little and it springs back. Bend it more and it stays bent. Bend it back and forth many times and it snaps. Springs and rubber bands are explored more in the unit 'Stretching and springs'.
examples: A thumbprint stays in clay. That is a plastic change.
A squeezed sponge springs back. It is elastic.
A papad snaps. It is brittle.
explanations.art: Three baskets labelled STAYS CHANGED, SPRINGS BACK and BREAKS, holding clay, a sponge and a broken papad.
explanations.context: Push three different things in the same way and you get three different results. This card names the three results.

explanations.concept: A bigger force makes a bigger change
explanations.definition: The bigger the force, the bigger the change of shape, until the thing breaks.
explanations.description: Drop a clay ball onto a plate from higher up, and it hits the plate faster. The plate has to push harder to stop it. That bigger push squashes it more. So the flat patch on the bottom gets wider. Engineers use this rule all the time. They push and pull on materials with machines, and measure exactly how much they change. The chart shows made-up results from the clay drop test in this unit.
examples: A gentle press makes a small dent in dough. A hard press makes a deep one.
A light child sitting on a cushion squashes it a little. A heavy grown-up squashes it more.
explanations.art: Four clay balls with flat patches getting wider, each under a small arrow that gets bigger.
explanations.context: Remember the clay drop test, where you drop clay balls from different heights? This card explains the pattern you find.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how wide the flat patch was after each drop
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.concept: Inside a bend: squashed and stretched at once
explanations.definition: When something bends, the inside of the curve is squashed and the outside is stretched. The middle is hardly changed at all.
explanations.description: Draw lines across a long sponge, then bend it. On the inside of the curve, the lines crowd together. On the outside, they spread apart. Every bending thing works like this, from a ruler to a bridge. So a thing resists bending best when it has lots of material far from its middle. A ruler lying flat bends easily. Stand it on its thin edge and it hardly bends at all, though it is the same ruler. Steel beams in buildings are shaped like the letter I for the same reason.
examples: Press the middle of a ruler lying flat, and it bends easily. Stand it on its edge, and the same press hardly bends it.
Steel beams in buildings and railway tracks have an I shape.
Bamboo is a hollow tube, so it is very stiff for how light it is.
explanations.art: A bent sponge with lines squeezed on the inside and spread on the outside, and beside it an I-shaped steel beam.
explanations.context: Remember the bendy sponge activity, where you drew lines on a sponge and bent it? This card explains what you saw.

explanations.definition: Changing the shape of a material can make it much stronger, without adding any more material. Folds, tubes and arches are the main tricks.
explanations.description: A flat sheet of paper sags under one coin. Fold the same sheet like a fan, and it can hold many coins. Each fold is a little stiff wall standing on its edge. Rolled tubes are strong too. Galileo, the Italian scientist, wrote about this in 1638. He noticed that hollow bones and hollow reeds are strong for how light they are. An arch carries a push along its curve, down to its two feet. The chart shows made-up results from the paper bridge challenge in this unit.
examples: Wavy tin roof sheets are much stiffer than flat ones.
The wavy layer inside cardboard boxes makes them strong.
An eggshell is a dome, a curved shell. It is very hard to crush by squeezing its two ends.
explanations.art: A flat paper sheet sagging under one coin next to a folded fan of paper holding a stack of coins.
explanations.context: Remember the paper bridge challenge, where one sheet of paper must hold coins over a gap? This card explains why folds help.

chart.title: Made-up example results: coins held by one sheet of paper
chart.y: Coins held before it sagged to the table
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.concept: Twisting, and how twists make rope
explanations.definition: A twist turns one end of a thing one way, while the other end turns the other way or stays still.
explanations.description: When you wring a wet towel, the twist squeezes the cloth tighter and tighter, and the water is pushed out. Thread and rope are made with twists too. Cotton wool is made of short fibres, each only about 2 to 4 centimetres long. Pull a loose strand of cotton wool, and the fibres slide apart. Twist the same cotton into a wick, and the twist squeezes the fibres against each other. Friction, the grip between touching things, then stops them sliding. So the twisted wick is far stronger. Every cotton thread is spun this way, on a charkha or in a mill. In Kerala, coir rope has been twisted from coconut husk fibres for centuries. You can read more about grip in the unit 'Friction'.
examples: Wringing out clothes on washing day.
A diya wick, twisted from cotton wool.
Coir rope, twisted from coconut fibres.
explanations.art: A loose wisp of cotton wool pulling apart, next to the same cotton twisted into a wick that holds up a small bag of coins.
explanations.context: Remember the twisting activity, where you wring a towel and twist cotton wool into a wick? This card explains how twisting works.

explanations.definition: A force can start a thing moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, or turn it in a new direction.
explanations.description: Think of one cricket ball. The bowler's push starts it and speeds it up. The bat's push turns the ball the other way. The grass slows it down. A fielder's hands stop it. Every one of these changes needs a force. The more mass a thing has, the bigger the force needed to change its speed or direction by the same amount. That is why a full trolley is harder to start and stop than an empty one. If no force acts, a moving thing keeps going at the same speed in a straight line. On Earth, friction and air usually slow things down, so we hardly ever see that. When two forces on a thing are equal and opposite, they cancel out, and its movement does not change. You can read about that in the unit 'Pushes and pulls'.
examples: A carrom striker hits a coin. The coin starts moving, and the striker slows and turns.
A kite string's tug turns the kite.
Brakes slow a bicycle.
explanations.art: One cricket ball's journey drawn as a dotted path: bowled, hit back, slowing on grass, caught, with an arrow at each force.
explanations.context: Forces don't only change shape. This card is about the other things they do to moving things.

explanations.definition: When a ball bounces, it squashes against the floor, then springs back. The springing back pushes it off in a new direction.
explanations.description: A ball hits the floor going down. The floor pushes up on it and squashes it a little flatter for a tiny moment, too fast to see. Then the ball springs back to round. As it does, it pushes down on the floor, and the floor pushes it back up. So the force that changed its direction also changed its shape. Wet the bottom of a tennis ball and drop it on newspaper. The wet circle shows how flat it got. Drop it from higher, and it hits faster and gets squashed flatter. A clay ball does not bounce at all. It stays squashed, so nothing pushes it back up. The chart shows made-up results from the wet ball print test.
examples: A tennis racket and a tennis ball both squash when they meet.
A cricket ball squashes a little against the bat.
A ball of dough lands with a flat thud and stays put.
explanations.art: A slow-motion strip of a tennis ball falling, squashing flat on the floor, and springing back up.
explanations.context: Remember the wet ball prints test, where you drop a wet ball on paper from different heights? This card explains what the prints show.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how wide the wet ball print was
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

explanations.concept: Going round needs a pull inwards
explanations.definition: To move in a circle, a thing needs a force that keeps pulling it towards the middle. That force keeps changing its direction.
explanations.description: Put a ball in a sock, tie a string to it, and swing it in a circle beside you. Your hand keeps pulling it inwards through the string, so it keeps turning. Let go, and it flies off in a straight line. The Moon goes round the Earth in the same way. The Earth's gravity keeps pulling it inwards. Isaac Newton, an English scientist, explained this in 1687. Without that pull, the Moon would fly off in a straight line into space. You can read more in the units about gravity.
examples: A merry-go-round pulls you inwards through the bar you hold.
A cyclist leans into a turn, so the road can push them round.
In a spinning washing machine, the drum pushes the clothes inwards, so they go round. The water goes straight on, out through the holes.
explanations.art: A child swinging a sock with a ball on a string, the string pulling inwards, and a dotted line where it flies off straight when let go.
explanations.context: Why does a thing go round in a circle? This card explains that a constant pull inwards keeps turning it.

explanations.concept: Deep down: atoms pushed together and pulled apart
explanations.definition: Everything is made of atoms held to each other by bonds. Bonds act a little like tiny springs. A shape changes when atoms are pushed closer or pulled further apart.
explanations.description: Press a steel spoon or a table, and its atoms are pushed slightly closer. Their bonds push back, so it springs back when you let go. That is elastic. A sponge and a rubber band spring back too, but in other ways. A sponge's thin walls bend and then straighten. A rubber band is made of long, tangled chains of atoms that straighten out when pulled, then curl up again. In metals, whole rows of atoms can slide past each other into new places, and stay there. In clay and dough, tiny grains slide past each other in the same way, held together by water. That is a plastic change. In 1934, three scientists explained how rows of atoms in metals slip, one small step at a time. They were Geoffrey Taylor, Egon Orowan and Michael Polanyi, working separately. In brittle things like glass, the atoms cannot slide. So the push gathers at the tip of a tiny scratch, and a crack races across. In 1921, an English engineer, Alan Griffith, showed that tiny scratches are what make glass weak. That is why a glass-cutter scratches a line first, then snaps the glass along it.
examples: A glass shop scratches a line on a sheet of glass, then snaps it cleanly along the line.
A gold bangle can be hammered thinner because rows of gold atoms slide without breaking.
explanations.art: Three zoomed-in grids of atoms: springs squashed then springing back, a row of atoms slipping one step sideways, and a crack opening at a scratch.
explanations.context: This card zooms in, far past anything a microscope can show. It explains why things spring back, stay changed or break.

explanations.description: Glass is hard like a solid. But its atoms are jumbled, like a liquid frozen in the middle of moving. In 1998, Edgar Zanotto, a Brazilian scientist, worked out that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to sag. But what glass really is remains a puzzle. In 1995, a famous American physicist, Philip Anderson, called it perhaps the deepest unsolved problem about solids.
examples: Old Roman glass bowls, about 2,000 years old, have not sagged at all.
A window pane at home is the same shape it was when it was made.

perspectives.explanation: Glass is a solid. Its atoms are jumbled, but they are stuck in place and do not flow.
Glass is best thought of as a liquid that has slowed down so much it cannot flow in any time we can measure.
Glass is its own kind of matter, neither a normal solid nor a liquid. Exactly why it goes stiff as it cools is still being studied.

explanations.art: A sheet of glass beside a zoom of jumbled glass atoms, with a question mark between them.
explanations.context: Glass is hard and brittle. This card is about a surprise: scientists still argue about what kind of stuff it is. The card on old church windows busts a popular myth about it.

explanations.concept: Living things grow to match the forces on them
explanations.definition: Bones, muscles and plants are alive. They slowly change shape and grow stronger where they are pushed and pulled, and weaker where they are not.
explanations.description: In 1892, a German doctor, Julius Wolff, wrote that bones reshape themselves to match the forces on them. The bones in a tennis player's playing arm grow thicker. Astronauts floating in space hardly press on their bones. So they can lose about 1 to 2 out of every 100 parts of their hip bones each month, and must exercise every day. Your spine squashes too. During the day, the soft pads between its bones are pressed down. So you are about 1 centimetre shorter at bedtime than when you wake up. Trees that sway in the wind grow thicker, sturdier trunks. In 1973, an American plant scientist, Mark Jaffe, gave this a name: thigmomorphogenesis. It means 'shape made by touch'. Trees tied too tightly to stakes grow weaker trunks.
examples: Children who run and jump grow stronger bones.
Trees on windy hilltops are short and thick.
You are a little taller in the morning than at night.
explanations.art: Three panels: an astronaut exercising on a treadmill with straps, a short thick tree bent by wind on a hill, and a child measured against a wall at morning and night.
explanations.context: Your body is shaped by forces too. This card is about how living things change shape, and grow stronger, when they are pushed and pulled.

explanations.definition: The giant slabs of Earth's outer layer, called tectonic plates, push on each other. Over millions of years, these pushes fold, crack and lift rock into mountains.
explanations.description: The plate that India sits on moves north by about 4 to 5 centimetres a year. That is about as fast as fingernails grow. About 50 million years ago, it began to crash into Asia. The rock crumpled up like a rug pushed against a wall. That is how the Himalayas formed, and they are still rising by a few millimetres a year. Rock also bends slowly, until it suddenly snaps. That snap is an earthquake. The spinning Earth changes shape too. Its spin makes it bulge at the middle. It is about 43 kilometres wider across the equator than from pole to pole. Even the solid ground under you rises and falls each day, by up to about 30 centimetres, as the Moon and Sun pull on it.
examples: Fossil sea shells are found high in the Himalayas. The rocks they lie in were once under the sea.
You can see bent and folded rock layers in road cuttings in hilly places.
explanations.art: India drawn as a slab pushing north into Asia, rock layers crumpled into the Himalayas, with a tiny fossil shell near the peaks.
explanations.context: Forces don't only shape small things. This card is about the pushes that fold mountains and squash the whole spinning Earth.

explanations.concept: Forces shape moons, stars and space itself
explanations.definition: Gravity can squeeze, stretch and heat whole worlds. Very strong gravity can even stretch and squash space itself.
explanations.description: Io is one of Jupiter's moons. Jupiter's huge gravity stretches and squeezes Io as it goes round. All that squeezing heats Io's insides. So Io has more active volcanoes than any other place we know. Some dead stars are squashed so hard that their atoms are crushed together. These are called neutron stars. A teaspoon of one would weigh about as much as a small mountain. Near a black hole, gravity can stretch a star apart. Astronomers have seen flashes of light from stars being torn up like this. Space itself can be stretched and squashed too. In 2015, the LIGO detectors in America measured a ripple in space from two black holes crashing together. As it passed, it stretched and squashed their 4-kilometre-long arms by an amount hundreds of times smaller than a proton. A proton is one of the particles in the centre of an atom.
examples: Io's volcanoes throw material hundreds of kilometres up into space.
LIGO is now joined by detectors in Italy and Japan. One is planned in India, called LIGO-India.
explanations.art: Jupiter's moon Io squeezed into a slight egg shape with volcanoes glowing, and behind it a net-like grid of space rippling.
explanations.context: This card follows shape-changing forces out into space, to moons, dead stars and space itself.

explanations.definition: Bend a stick of dry spaghetti until it snaps, and it nearly always breaks into three or more pieces, not two.
explanations.description: The famous physicist Richard Feynman once spent an evening trying to snap spaghetti into just two pieces. He could not. In 2005, two French scientists, Basile Audoly and Sébastien Neukirch, explained why. When the first break happens, the two halves spring back. That sends a wave of extra bending racing along each half, and it snaps them again. In 2018, a team at MIT in America found a trick. Twist the spaghetti about three-quarters of a turn or more first, then bend it slowly. Then it can snap into just two pieces. So a twist changes how a bend breaks.
examples: Snap dry spaghetti, a thin dry stick or dry noodles. Count the pieces.
Then try twisting it about three-quarters of a turn before bending, and see what happens.
explanations.art: A stick of spaghetti bent into a curve snapping into three pieces, with little flying bits, and beside it a twisted stick snapping neatly in two.
explanations.context: Here is a puzzle you can try in your kitchen. Scientists only explained it in 2005.

agreed.text: Forces can change the shape of things, by squashing, stretching, twisting or bending.
agreed.evidence: Anyone can see it with dough, sponges and rubber bands. Engineers measure it in every material, with machines that push and pull.

agreed.text: Materials answer forces in different ways. Some keep the new shape, some spring back, and some break.
agreed.evidence: Clay, sponge and glass all react differently to the same push. Engineers choose materials for this reason, like rubber for tyres and steel for bridges.

agreed.text: Everything changes shape a little when pushed, even steel and stone.
agreed.evidence: Tall buildings sway in the wind. Bridges sag a little when trucks cross. Scientists can show a table bending under a gentle press by bouncing a laser beam off a mirror lying on it.

agreed.text: A force is needed to change a thing's speed or direction.
agreed.evidence: Isaac Newton wrote this down in 1687. Every spacecraft is steered using his rules, and they arrive where they are meant to.

agreed.text: The spinning Earth bulges at the equator.
agreed.evidence: Measurements from satellites show the Earth is about 43 kilometres wider across the equator than from pole to pole.

challenging.claim: Hard things like steel and stone don't change shape when you push them.
challenging.who: Most of us think this without noticing.
challenging.for: We cannot see a steel table or a stone wall change shape when we press it.
challenging.against: They do change, just too little to see. A laser beam bounced off a mirror on a table moves when someone presses the table. Bridges sag when trucks cross them. The Himalayas are bent rock.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that hard things never change shape.

challenging.claim: Old church windows are thicker at the bottom because glass slowly flows downwards.
challenging.for: Some very old windows really are thicker at the bottom. And glass atoms are jumbled like a liquid's.
challenging.against: Some old windows are thicker at the top or the side. They were made unevenly, and builders often put the thick edge at the bottom. Roman glass 2,000 years old has not sagged. In 1998, Edgar Zanotto worked out that glass at room temperature would take far longer than the age of the universe to flow.
challenging.context: Glass is hard but its atoms are jumbled. This card is about a popular story that glass slowly flows.

challenging.claim: If something isn't moving, no forces are acting on it.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: If nothing moves, it seems as if nothing is happening.
challenging.against: A book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table, all the time. The forces are equal and opposite, so they cancel. Push on a wall and it doesn't move, but you can feel the force. And the wall changes shape a tiny bit.
challenging.context: This card is about forces on things that are standing still.

challenging.claim: To make something stronger, you must make it thicker or use more material.
challenging.for: A thick stick is harder to break than a thin one.
challenging.against: Shape matters as much as amount. One sheet of paper folded like a fan holds many coins. Galileo pointed out in 1638 that hollow bones and reeds are strong for how light they are. Bamboo, bicycle frames and steel I-beams use the same trick.
challenging.context: This card is about whether stronger always means thicker.

challenging.claim: Mountains are fixed and never change shape.
challenging.who: An everyday idea. Mountains look as if they have always been there.
challenging.for: In a whole human lifetime, a mountain looks exactly the same.
challenging.against: The Himalayas are still rising by a few millimetres a year, as India pushes into Asia. Fossil sea shells high in the mountains show the rock was once under the sea. Earthquakes are rock snapping after bending.
challenging.context: This card is about whether mountains really stay the same.

challenging.claim: The science of how materials bend and stretch was built only by men, like Robert Hooke and Augustin Cauchy.
challenging.for: Hooke, Navier, Cauchy and others did write much of the theory, and most famous names in the story are men.
challenging.against: Sophie Germain, a French woman, taught herself mathematics in secret. She first wrote to scientists under a man's name, 'Monsieur LeBlanc'. In 1816 she won a top prize from the Paris Academy of Sciences, for maths about how bent and shaken metal plates vibrate. At first, as a woman, she was not allowed to attend the Academy's meetings. Her work had gaps, which others later filled, so historians still debate how much credit she should get.
challenging.context: This card is about who gets credit for the science of bending and stretching.

challenging.claim: Bones are dead and hard, like chalk.
challenging.who: A common idea, because skeletons look dry and stony
challenging.for: Bones are hard, and old skeletons in museums are dead.
challenging.against: Inside you, bones are alive. They have blood and cells that build and remove bone. They grow thicker where they are pushed most. Astronauts in space lose bone because it is not pushed. A broken bone heals itself.
challenging.context: This card is about whether your bones are alive and can change shape.

big_questions.q: Does a steel table change shape when a fly lands on it?
big_questions.hint: A bigger force makes a bigger change. So does a very tiny force make a very tiny change, or none at all?

big_questions.q: Why does a sponge spring back but dough stays squashed? What is different inside them?
big_questions.hint: Look closely at a sponge. It is full of holes with thin walls. What happens to those walls when you squeeze? What happens inside dough when it moves?

big_questions.q: Your bones grow stronger where they are pushed. How does a bone sense where it is being pushed?
big_questions.hint: Bone cells can sense being squeezed and stretched. Scientists are still finding out exactly how they decide where to build more bone.

big_questions.q: If you protected something from every push and pull, would it stay strong?
big_questions.hint: What happens to astronauts' bones in space? What happens to a tree tied tightly to a stake?

big_questions.q: When a ball bounces, where does its movement go while it is squashed flat for a moment?
big_questions.hint: A squashed sponge pushes back on your hand. Could the squashed ball be holding its movement for a moment, then giving it back?

big_questions.q: The Himalayas are still rising. Will they keep getting taller for ever?
big_questions.hint: Rain, ice and rivers are wearing them down at the same time. Which do you think will win?

big_questions.q: Is anything in the universe completely rigid, so that it never changes shape at all?
big_questions.hint: Even space itself stretches when a gravitational wave passes. Can you think of anything that can't change?

big_questions.q: A potter, a goldsmith, a baker and a blacksmith all change shapes with force. Why do we call some of this 'art' and some 'work'?
big_questions.hint: Who decides? Is rolling a perfect round chapati an art?

big_questions.q: Some sculptors say a statue is already hidden inside the stone. Is a shape something we make, or something we find?
big_questions.hint: When you squash dough, is the new shape new, or was it always possible?

big_questions.q: Why does dry spaghetti almost never break into just two pieces?
big_questions.hint: When it first snaps, both halves spring back fast. What might that sudden spring do?

story.title: The Bridge That Was Allowed to Sway
story.note: The living root bridges of Meghalaya are real. Khasi and Jaintia people grow them from the roots of rubber fig trees, sometimes guiding the roots through hollow betel-nut trunks, and some have been used for well over a hundred years. Iba, Kong Kyrmen and the young bridge are made up. Trees that are swayed by wind really do grow thicker, sturdier stems. Whether root bridges grow thicker exactly where they are walked on has not been carefully measured. In the story it is a guess based on how trees behave.
text: In the hills of Meghalaya, in the north-east of India, it rains more than almost anywhere else on Earth. Below the town of Sohra, a stream runs through a deep green gorge. Across it hangs a bridge that nobody built with a hammer. It was grown. Its floor and its rails are the living roots of a rubber fig tree, as thick as a man's leg, knotted together and furred with moss. People have walked across it for longer than anyone can remember.

Iba was nine, and she was in a hurry. Upstream, her aunt, Kong Kyrmen, was growing a new bridge. She had laid a hollow betel-nut trunk across the water like a long wooden gutter. Inside it, young roots from a fig tree on the bank were creeping across. They were pale and bendy, like cooked noodles.
'When will it be ready?' Iba asked.
'When you are as old as I am,' said Kong Kyrmen. 'Maybe older.'

Iba could not wait that long, so she decided to help. The young roots swung about in the wind. Where the gutter ended, they drooped and wandered. They looked untidy, like hair that had not been combed. So one morning Iba cut strips of cane and tied each root tightly to a straight bamboo pole. She tied them so well that they could not wobble at all.
'There,' she said. 'Now you will grow straight and strong.'
Her aunt looked at the tied roots for a long time. She did not untie them. 'Let us see,' she said.
On the far side, a few roots had escaped her. They hung loose over the water. Every gust pushed them about.

Then the monsoon came. Rain blew sideways off the hills. The stream roared brown and white. Every day after school, Iba ran up the path to check her bridge. The loose roots were thrashed and bent and tugged by the wind. Iba felt sorry for them. She tied her own roots even tighter, so the storm could not touch them.

The rains ended. The cold season came, bright and dry. One morning Iba took a piece of thread to measure her roots. She wrapped it round a tied root and pinched the thread where the ends met. Then she did the same with one of the wild roots on the far side. She held the two threads side by side.

The thread from the wild root was nearly twice as long. The tied roots were still pale and thin, as thin as the day she had tied them. The wild roots had grown thick and brown, with tough, wrinkled skin like her aunt's wrists.
'That's not fair,' Iba said. Her voice wobbled. 'I looked after mine.'

Kong Kyrmen did not laugh. She took Iba's hand and walked her down the slippery steps to the old bridge. 'Put your hand here,' she said. She pressed Iba's palm onto the roots in the middle, where the floor sagged lowest. That was where every foot had stepped for a hundred years. The roots there were the thickest of all. They had grown into each other until she could not tell where one ended and the next began.

'This is where it is pushed the most,' she said. 'Every time someone walks across, the roots bend a little and stretch a little. And they answer. They grow.' She tapped Iba's tied roots on the way back up. 'A root that is never pushed has no reason to grow.'

Iba thought about the bamboo behind her house. In the storms they bent nearly to the ground, then sprang back. She thought about the dry stick she had snapped for the fire, which could not bend at all. She thought about her own legs. They used to ache on the steep steps to school. Now they ran up without stopping.

That evening, she cut the cane. The roots sprang free and swayed a little in the breeze, as if they were stretching after a long sleep. It felt strange to let them go, like letting go of a little brother's hand at the edge of a road.

The next day she did something else. She wove a tiny basket and hung it from the young roots, with one smooth river stone inside. The roots dipped under it, and swung. 'Something to carry,' she told them. Every week she added one more stone. Every week the roots bent down a little further. And every week, when she measured with her thread, they were a little thicker.
Kong Kyrmen watched her. 'Now,' she said, 'you are building.'
Years went by. The roots crossed the stream and wrapped round a tree on the other side. Kong Kyrmen laid flat stones between them for a floor. Her hair turned white. Iba grew tall.

When Iba was nineteen, the young bridge was finally strong enough to hold a child. She was standing on the bank, wondering who should be the first to cross, when a small boy from the next village ran straight past her. He did not ask anyone. He ran out onto the roots.
The bridge dipped under his feet. It swayed, and creaked, and sprang back. The boy laughed out loud.
Iba opened her mouth to shout at him. Then she closed it again. She watched the roots bend under his weight and stretch, and come back. Under her breath, she said one word to them. 'Grow.'
story.epiphany: For the parent: every push and pull changes the shape of what it touches, even a little. The wind bends the roots, and a stone in a basket stretches them. Living things respond to those changes by growing stronger where they are pushed and pulled. Iba's tight ties protected the roots from every force, so they had no reason to grow, and stayed thin. Trees staked too tightly, and astronauts' bones in space, behave the same way. The bamboo that bends and the stick that snaps also hint at the difference between elastic and brittle.
ask: In the story, Iba tied the young roots so they could not move. Why did they stay thin?
The wild roots were thrashed by the storm. Why did they grow thicker?
Where were the roots thickest on the old bridge? Why there?
Why did Iba hang a basket of stones from the roots?
Iba nearly shouted at the boy, but didn't. Why do you think she stopped?
Iba's legs stopped aching on the steep steps. Which part of your body got stronger because you used it a lot?

games.title: Squash, Stretch, Twist or Bend?

printables.title: 24 action cards to cut out
items: Rolling a chapati with a rolling pin
A bamboo in a strong wind
Winding a rubber band round and round a pencil
Squeezing toothpaste out of the tube
A diver standing on a diving board
Twisting coconut fibres into coir rope
Stretching a hair band onto your hair
A cricket ball hitting the bat
Twisting a long balloon into the shape of a dog
TEST IT: squeeze a sponge, then let go. What happens?
TEST IT: bend a paper clip a little, then a lot. What happens each time?
TEST IT: twist a strip of paper with lines drawn across it, then let go. What happens to the lines?
TEST IT: press a biscuit gently between two fingers, harder and harder. What happens?

printables.title: Answer tokens: 3 for each player, for up to 4 players (12 tokens)

rules: Cut out the 24 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down in a pile. Keep score on a sheet of paper.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud. Act it out with your hands.
Put the card on the mat that fits: SQUASH, STRETCH, TWIST or BEND. Some cards fit two mats. Choose one and say why.
Then everyone shows one of their answer tokens at the same time. After the force stops, does the thing stay changed, spring back, or break?
Everyone who shows the right token scores one point. The player who placed the card scores one more for a good reason. If players disagree, a grown-up decides, using the notes in the steps.
A TEST IT card goes on no mat. Everyone does the test together. The first player to explain the result scores two points.
When the cards run out, the player with the most points wins. Players with the same points share the win.
