flow.do: 1. Lay the four mats on the floor. 2. Shuffle the 24 cards and put them face down. 3. Give each player their three answer tokens. 4. Get a sheet of paper for the score.
flow.say: A force is a push or a pull. It can squash, stretch, twist or bend things. Each card shows a force changing a shape. You decide which kind.
flow.kid: Put the four mats on the floor. Mix up the cards. Put them face down. Each card shows a force changing a shape.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squash, Stretch, Twist or Bend game. It is a card game about the ways forces change shape. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'Wringing out a wet towel'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Practice card. Wringing out a wet towel. Which mat? And when you let go, does the towel stay twisted, spring back, or break?
flow.kid: Practice card: wringing a wet towel. Which mat does it go on? Say your answer.

ask.q: Why does the towel go on the TWIST mat?
good: My hands turn opposite ways.
One end turns one way and the other end turns the other way.

check.q: Wringing out a wet towel is mostly…
check.why: A twist, and the player who placed it scores a point. Your two hands turn opposite ways. Picking 'squash' is close, because the twist squeezes the water out, but the action itself is a twist.

flow.do: 1. Take turns. Each player reads a card, acts it out and places it on a mat. 2. Everyone shows an answer token. 3. Write the points on the score sheet.
flow.say: Show me the force with your hands first. Then put it on a mat. Now everyone, does it stay changed, spring back, or break?
flow.kid: Take turns. Read your card. Act it out. Put it on a mat. Then hold up a token. Stays changed, springs back, or breaks?
flow.parent: Tricky cards: the chapati is a squash and a stretch, and it stays changed. The diving board bends, then springs back. The sitar string is stretched, and springs back. The wound rubber band springs back. The bangle stays changed, and so does the balloon dog. The papad and the apple break. The can stays squashed.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, stop and do the test together. Everyone guesses first.
flow.say: Before we test it, everyone guess what will happen. Then let's try it.
flow.kid: A TEST IT card! Guess first. Then do the test. Were you right?

ask.q: The paper clip sprang back after a small bend, but stayed bent after a big one. Why?
good: A small force lets it spring back.
A big force changes it for good.
A big bend makes rows of atoms inside slide to new places.

flow.think: Can the same thing be elastic and plastic? What decides which one it is?

flow.do: 1. Add up the points to find the winner. 2. Look at the four mats together.
flow.say: Which mat got the most cards? Which kind of shape change do we use most at home?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Who won? Which mat has the most cards? Why do you think that is?
flow.think: Which jobs at home need things that stay changed? Which need things that spring back?

games.context: This is a card game about the four ways forces change shape: squash, stretch, twist and bend. Players also guess whether each thing stays changed, springs back or breaks.

games.title: Six Things a Force Can Do
games.players: 2 to 4 players, in any room with some clear floor
rules: Put the object cards face down. Put the real objects nearby. You also need one dice, for example from a Ludo set.
On your turn, roll the dice and take an object card. The dice chart tells you what your force must do.
If the object is not moving and the dice says stop, slow down, speed up or turn, first start it moving with a push. Then do the job.
Use a push or a pull to do it to the object. For example, "turn it" with a toy car.
Say whether you used a push or a pull. Write it on the force log. Everyone shares one force log.
If the others agree you did it, you win a point. If it is impossible, explain why, and you still win a point.
Put your card back at the bottom of the pile. After everyone has had 3 turns, the player with the most points wins. Players with the same points share the win.

setup.art: A dice face chart with six pictures: start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn, change shape.
setup.caption: 1. Put the dice chart where everyone can see it.

setup.art: A child rolling a dice beside a pile of object cards, with a ball, a balloon, a toy car and dough on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the dice and take an object card.

setup.art: A child gently tapping a rolling toy car from the side so it turns, an arrow showing the push.
setup.caption: 3. Use a push or a pull to do what the dice says.

flow.do: 1. Put the real objects on the floor. 2. Put the object cards face down. 3. Put the dice chart where everyone can see it.
flow.say: A force is a push or a pull. Forces can do six things. Start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn, and change shape. Let's do all six.
flow.kid: Forces can do six things. Start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn, change shape. Let's try them all!
flow.context: This is the first step of Six Things a Force Can Do. It is a game where you use pushes and pulls to make objects do what a dice says.

flow.do: Do a practice turn with the soft ball. Roll the ball gently towards your child. Ask them to do each of the six things to it, one after another.
flow.say: Here comes the ball. Stop it. Now start it. Speed it up. Slow it down. Turn it. Now change its shape.
flow.kid: Roll a soft ball. Stop it. Start it. Speed it up. Slow it down. Turn it. Squeeze it!

ask.q: How did you turn the ball?
good: I pushed it from the side.
I tapped it so it went a new way.

check.q: You catch a rolling ball and hold it still. Which of the six things did your hands do?
check.why: Your hands pushed against the ball's movement and stopped it, so you win the practice point. Your hands also squashed the ball a tiny bit, so a stop can change a shape too.

flow.do: 1. Take turns rolling the dice and taking a card. 2. Each player does the action to that object. 3. They say push or pull and fill in the force log. 4. Everyone has 3 turns.
flow.say: What did the dice say? How will you do that to this object? Was it a push or a pull?
flow.kid: Roll the dice. Take a card. Do what the dice says to that object. Push or pull? Write it down.
flow.parent: Some turns are puzzles. Speeding up a bowl of water: stir it faster. Changing the shape of a carrom coin: almost impossible by hand. That is a good answer if explained, because hard things need enormous forces to change shape. Turning a sheet of paper: blow on it from the side. One action can do two jobs. A kick from the side turns a ball and speeds it up.

flow.do: Look at the force logs together. Count how many pushes and how many pulls were used.
flow.say: Did we use more pushes or more pulls? Was there any job we couldn't do?
flow.kid: Look at your force log. More pushes or more pulls? Which job was hardest?
flow.think: When you catch a ball, your hands stop it and squash it a tiny bit. Can one force do two jobs at once?

games.context: This is a movement game about the six things a force can do: start, stop, speed up, slow down, turn, and change shape. A dice decides which one you must do.

items.p: You press a ball of dough flat with your hand. Which shape change is this?
items.why: Pressing inwards on something makes it flatter. That is a squash. Picking 'stretch' is close, because the dough also spreads wider. But your push is inwards, so it is mainly a squash.
items.art: A hand pressing a dough ball flat.

items.p: You wring water out of a wet towel. Which shape change is this?
items.why: Your two hands turn opposite ways. That is a twist. Picking 'squash' makes sense, because the twist does squeeze the water out. But the action itself is twisting.

items.p: When you pull a rubber band, it gets longer. This is called a ____.
items.why: Pulling outwards on something makes it longer. That is a stretch.

items.p: Sort these. After the force stops, does each one stay changed or spring back?
items.a: see items
items.why: Clay, dough and cans keep their new shapes. Sponges, rubber bands and cushions are elastic, so they spring back.

items.p: A papad snaps when you bend it. A word for things that break instead of bending is…
items.why: Brittle things crack and break instead of bending. Picking 'plastic' often comes from thinking of plastic bottles. In science, plastic means 'stays changed'.

items.p: In science, a 'plastic' change means the thing keeps its new shape after the force stops.
items.why: True. Scientists use 'plastic' to mean 'stays changed', like clay. It is not about the stuff bottles are made of.

items.p: In the clay drop test, you drop the same clay ball from 10 cm and from 80 cm. Which drop makes the wider flat patch?
items.why: From higher up, the ball hits the plate faster. The plate pushes back harder, so it squashes the clay more. Picking 'both the same' means thinking the same clay must always squash the same amount. But from higher up, the push from the plate is bigger.
items.context: In the clay drop test, you drop equal clay balls onto a steel plate from different heights. Then you measure the flat patch on the bottom of each.

items.p: A batter in a cricket match hits the ball back the way it came. What did the force from the bat change?
items.why: The bat sent the ball back the other way, usually faster than before. The ball was also squashed a tiny bit. Picking 'only shape' notices the squash but misses the change in movement.

items.p: A force can make a moving thing faster or slower, but it can never make it go a different way.
items.why: False. A push from the side turns a moving thing. Kick a rolling football from the side, and it goes off a new way. Speed and direction can both be changed by a force.

items.p: A carrom coin slides across the board and hits the edge. Which way does it go next?
opts: Back into the board, because the edge pushed it
It stops dead and never moves again
It goes back the way it came, even if it hit at a slant
items.why: The edge pushes back on the coin, so the coin changes direction. If it hits at a slant, it goes off at a slant the other way, like light off a mirror. Picking 'stops dead' happens sometimes on a slow shot. But a fast coin is turned, not stopped.
items.art: A carrom coin sliding at a slant, bouncing off the edge of the board.

items.p: Match each job to the shape change it uses most.
pairs: Pulling a hair band onto your hair
Twisting coconut fibres into coir rope
A diving board when you stand on its end
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Rolling presses the dough flat. A hair band is pulled longer. Coir fibres are twisted into rope. A diving board curves down.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, rolls a ball across the floor. It slows down and stops. She says, 'It stopped by itself. Nothing pushed it.' What is wrong with her idea? What was pushing on the ball?
items.a: A strong answer says that a moving thing only slows down if a force acts on it. Here the floor rubs on the ball, which is friction, and the air pushes on it a little too. On a smoother floor the ball rolls further, which shows the floor was slowing it.
items.why: Things do not stop by themselves. Every change in movement, including stopping, needs a push or a pull. This was Aristotle's mistake too, and Galileo showed it.

items.p: Why does a sponge spring back but clay stays squashed? Give your best idea.
items.a: Any thoughtful idea. A good one: a sponge is full of holes with thin, springy walls. They bend when you squeeze, then straighten. In clay, tiny pieces slide to new places and stay there.
items.why: Elastic things spring back into shape. In a plastic change, the tiny pieces inside move to new places and stay.

items.p: Look at your own results from the clay drop test. Which drop made the widest patch? Was that what you guessed? Name one thing that could have made your test unfair.
items.a: A strong answer gives a real number, for example 'the 80 cm drop made a patch 4 cm wide'. It says whether the guess was right. It names one thing that might have changed by mistake, for example a ball that was bigger, or a throw instead of a drop.
items.why: Using your own numbers is how scientists check an idea. Spotting what could have gone wrong makes the next test better.
items.context: In the clay drop test, you drop equal clay balls onto a steel plate from different heights. Then you measure the flat patch on the bottom of each.

items.p: Draw a tennis ball at the moment it hits a cricket bat. Show how the ball's shape changes. Draw an arrow for the bat's push on the ball.
items.a: A strong drawing shows the ball flattened on the side touching the bat. The arrow starts at the bat and points into the ball, back the way the ball came. The best drawings say the ball will then spring back and fly off the other way.
items.why: One push from the bat does two jobs. It squashes the ball and it turns the ball round. Shape and movement change together.

items.p: A school in Chennai is choosing a floor for under the swings. Three people say what they think.

views.says: Concrete is best. It does not change shape, it lasts for years, and it is easy to sweep.
Thick rubber mats are best. When a child falls, the mat squashes, so the child stops more slowly and gently.
Deep sand is best. It squashes and spreads when you land, and it costs very little. But it must be raked every day.

items.ask: Which floor would you choose? Give a reason about what squashes and what does not. Then say one fair point from someone you disagree with.
items.a: A strong answer picks a floor and explains it with shape changes: a floor that squashes makes a fall stop more slowly, so the push on the child is smaller. It then admits a real point from another side, for example that concrete is cheap and lasts, or that sand needs raking and can hide rubbish.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A floor that changes shape is kinder in a fall, but it costs more or needs more care. Real playgrounds weigh up both.

items.p: In these made-up clay drop results, every time the height doubles, the patch gets 1 cm wider. Predict how wide the patch would be from 160 cm: ____ cm.
items.why: 160 cm is double 80 cm. From 80 cm the patch was 4 cm, so one more doubling adds 1 cm. 4 + 1 = 5 cm. A real test would show whether the pattern keeps going.
items.context: In the clay drop test, you drop equal clay balls onto a steel plate from different heights. Then you measure the flat patch on the bottom of each.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how wide the flat patch was after each drop
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

items.p: In the bendy sponge activity, you bend a sponge with lines drawn across it. What happens to the lines on the INSIDE of the curve?
items.why: The inside of a bend is squashed, so the lines crowd together. The outside is stretched, so they spread apart. Picking 'spread apart' mixes up the inside with the outside.
items.context: In the bendy sponge activity, you draw straight lines across a long sponge, then bend it into a curve.

items.p: You press the middle of a plastic ruler lying flat, and it bends easily. Stand the same ruler on its thin edge, and the same press hardly bends it. Why?
opts: On its edge, more of the ruler is far from the middle of the bend
items.why: On its edge, the top and bottom of the ruler are far apart. The top must squash and the bottom must stretch a lot to bend it, so it resists. Picking 'the ruler got harder' means looking for a change in the material. Only its position changed.
items.context: In the bendy sponge activity, you also press the middle of a ruler laid across two tins, first lying flat and then standing on its edge.

items.p: Sort these by what happens after a strong force. Stays changed, springs back, or breaks?
items.a: see items
items.why: Gold and steel can be bent or hammered into new shapes. Tennis balls and bamboo spring back. Glass and dry biscuits are brittle.

items.p: A metal hair clip that springs back after a small bend will spring back however hard you bend it.
items.why: False. A small bend is elastic, so the clip springs back. A big bend is plastic, so the clip stays bent. The same thing can be elastic for a small force and plastic for a big one.

items.p: Why do steel beams in buildings often have an I shape?
opts: Most of the steel is at the top and bottom, where a bend squashes and stretches most
It looks like the letter I for 'iron'
items.why: A bend squashes the top and stretches the bottom most. So steel placed there resists bending best, without wasting steel in the middle. Picking 'iron' is a fun guess, but the shape is about bending, not spelling.

items.p: Why is cotton wool twisted into a wick stronger than the same cotton pulled into a loose strand?
opts: The twist squeezes the fibres together, so friction stops them sliding apart
items.why: Twisting presses the short fibres against each other. Friction, the grip between touching things, holds them together, so they share the pull. Picking 'longer fibres' is a sensible guess, but each fibre stays the same length.
items.context: In the twisting activity, you pull a loose strand of cotton wool, then twist the same amount into a wick, and hang a bag of coins from it.

items.p: A ball is swung round on a string. The string breaks. Which way does the ball go?
opts: Straight on, in the direction it was moving
It keeps going round in a circle
items.why: With no string pulling it inwards, nothing turns it any more. So it flies off in a straight line. Picking 'keeps going round' is a very common idea. But going round needs a pull inwards all the time.

items.p: Ananya, a girl in Class 4, says, 'A steel table is so hard that pressing it changes nothing at all.' What would you tell her? Describe the evidence from the laser and mirror activity.
items.a: A strong answer says that every push changes a thing's shape a little, even steel. It describes the evidence: a laser dot bounced off a mirror on the table moves when someone presses the table, so the table must have bent. It says the bend is too small to see with our eyes.
items.why: Hard things change shape too, only by tiny amounts. The laser makes the tiny bend big enough to see.
items.context: In the laser and mirror activity, a small mirror lies on a table. A laser pointer shines on the mirror, and the beam bounces onto the wall as a dot.

items.p: You drop a clay ball and a rubber ball from the same height onto the floor. Both squash when they land. Only the rubber ball comes back up. Explain why.
items.a: A strong answer says that both balls squash, but the rubber ball is elastic. It springs back into shape, and that pushes on the floor, so the floor pushes it back up. The clay is plastic. It stays squashed, so nothing pushes it up again.
items.why: A bounce is a squash and a spring back. Without the spring back, there is no bounce.
items.context: In the wet ball prints test, you drop a wet ball onto newspaper. The size of the wet circle shows how much the ball squashed when it landed.

items.p: Put these in order, from EASIEST to change the shape of by hand, to HARDEST: a stone, a rubber eraser, a steel spoon, dough.
items.a: order shown
items.why: Dough squashes with a light press. A rubber eraser needs a firm squeeze. A steel spoon needs a strong push to bend. A stone hardly changes at all by hand.

items.p: A rubber band hangs from a hook. You hang a small bag from it and add coins one at a time. You want a fair test of whether more coins stretch the band longer. Write what you will change, what you will measure, and what you will keep the same.
items.a: I will change the number of coins. I will measure how long the rubber band is each time. I will keep the same rubber band, the same bag, the same hook, and measure from the same starting point.
items.why: A fair test changes one thing and keeps the rest the same.

items.p: A ball of dough is being squashed between your two hands. Show the forces on it, with one arrow for each.
items.obj: a ball of dough squashed between two hands
items.why: Each hand pushes inwards, towards the dough. Two pushes towards each other make a squash. Gravity also pulls the dough down.

items.p: Design a sandal sole that can bend when you walk but never snaps. Label which parts squash and which parts stretch when it bends.
items.a: Any thoughtful design. The top of the bend is squashed and the bottom is stretched, or the other way round when it bends the other way. Soft rubber, or grooves across the sole, help it bend.
items.why: A bend squashes one side and stretches the other.
items.art: An empty sandal-sole outline, bent slightly.

items.p: A girl in Madurai must post a glass bottle of homemade pickle to her aunt in Pune. Her friends each suggest a way to pack it.

views.who: Nandini, who works at the post office
views.says: Use a thick, stiff cardboard box with no gaps. It spreads a knock over the whole box, and nothing sharp can poke through to the glass.
Wrap it in bubble wrap. The bubbles squash and spring back, so they slow a bump down gently.
Crumple old newspaper round it. The paper squashes and stays squashed, so it soaks up the bump, and it costs nothing.

items.ask: Which way would you choose? Use the words squash, spring back or stays changed in your reason. Then say one thing another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a way and explains it with shape changes. Squashing material makes a bump stop more slowly, so the push on the glass is smaller. It answers back fairly, for example that a stiff box stops sharp corners poking in, or that newspaper works only once because it stays squashed. The best answers may mix two ways.
items.why: Each way is used for real. Stiff boxes spread out a push, bubble wrap springs back for many bumps, and crumpled paper is cheap but works only once. This is the same thinking as the Save the Egg challenge.

items.p: Deep down, why does a steel ruler spring back after a small bend?
opts: Its atoms are pushed closer on one side and pulled apart on the other, and the bonds between them pull them back
Air inside it pushes it back
items.why: Bonds between atoms act a little like tiny springs. Squash them or stretch them, and they pull the atoms back into place. Picking 'air inside' is a sensible guess for a sponge, but a steel ruler has no air holes. Bending does not make atoms bigger. It moves them closer or further apart.

items.p: A steel ruler springs back after a small bend. This means its atoms moved to new places and stayed there.
items.why: False. When a steel ruler springs back, its atoms were only pushed closer or pulled apart a little, and the bonds pulled them back. Atoms that slide to new places and stay there give a plastic change, like a bent paper clip.

items.p: A gold bangle can be hammered into a new shape without breaking. A glass bangle cannot. Why?
opts: In gold, rows of atoms can slide past each other. In glass they cannot, so cracks spread
Glass is not made of atoms
items.why: In metals, rows of atoms slip into new places one step at a time. In glass the atoms are jumbled and stuck, so a push gathers at tiny scratches and a crack races across. Picking 'gold is heavier' links strength with weight, but that is not the reason.

items.p: Why does a glass shop scratch a line on glass before snapping it?
opts: The scratch is where a crack starts, so it breaks along the line
The scratch makes the glass softer
items.why: Alan Griffith showed in 1921 that tiny scratches make glass weak, because the push gathers at their tips. A scratched line makes the crack go exactly where the glass-cutter wants. Picking 'softer' mixes up weak with soft.

items.p: Astronauts living in space for months lose some of their bone. Why?
opts: Floating, they hardly push on their bones, so the bones do not need to stay strong
Space air is poisonous to bones
Their bones melt in the cold
items.why: Bones reshape to match the forces on them. With almost no pushing, the body removes bone it doesn't seem to need. That is why astronauts exercise for about two hours a day. Picking 'cold' is a guess about space, but the space station is kept warm.

items.p: Ritu, a girl in Class 4, measures her height against a wall. In the morning she is 128.5 cm. At bedtime she is 127.5 cm. Her brother Arun says, 'Your tape must be wrong.' Is he right? Explain.
items.a: A strong answer says the tape is probably fine. During the day, Ritu's weight squashes the soft pads between the bones of her spine, so she gets about 1 cm shorter. At night, lying down, the pads spring back. To check, she could measure the same way on a few days and see if it happens each time.
items.why: People really are about 1 cm taller in the morning. Repeating a measurement is how you tell a real change from a mistake.
items.context: In the morning and night project, you measure your height against a wall as soon as you wake up, and again at bedtime.

items.p: Fossil sea shells are found high in the Himalayas. What does this tell us?
opts: The rock was once under the sea, and was pushed up by enormous forces
The sea was once as high as the mountains
items.why: The plate India sits on pushed into Asia and crumpled the old sea floor up into mountains. Picking 'the sea was once that high' is a natural guess. But it was the land that rose, not the sea.

items.p: The plate that India sits on moves north by about 5 cm a year. In 20 years it moves about ____ cm.
items.why: 20 lots of 5 cm is 100 cm. That is 1 metre. 5 × 20 = 100.

answer_chart.title: How far India's plate moves, at about 5 cm a year

items.p: The spinning Earth is about 43 km wider across the equator than from pole to pole. What causes the bulge?
opts: Its spin makes the middle bulge out a little
The equator is hotter, so it swells
items.why: As the Earth spins, the rock at the equator moves fastest, and it swings outwards a little. So the middle bulges out and the poles are a little flatter. Picking 'hotter' is a clever guess, since heat does swell things. But it is the spin.
items.context: The Earth is not a perfect ball. It is a little wider across the middle.

answer_chart.title: How wide the Earth is, measured two ways

data.label: Pole to pole, through the middle
Across the equator, through the middle

answer_chart.note: The difference is about 43 kilometres. The bars look nearly the same, because 43 is tiny next to 12,700.

items.p: Match each change to what happens to the atoms inside. Atoms are the tiny pieces that everything is made of.
pairs: A steel wire stretched a little, then let go
atoms pulled a little apart, then pulled back
A gold bangle hammered into a new shape
rows of atoms slide to new places and stay
A glass bangle dropped on the floor
a crack races between the atoms
A rubber eraser squeezed, then let go
long chains of atoms bunch up, then spring back
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Springing back means the atoms return to their places. Staying changed means rows of atoms have slid. Breaking means a crack has opened between atoms.

items.p: People who build bridges do not all agree on whether a bridge should bend.

views.who: Meenakshi, an engineer who builds steel road bridges
views.says: A bridge should be stiff. If it sways, people feel unsafe, and metal that bends over and over can crack.

views.who: Kong Kyrmen, who grows living root bridges in Meghalaya
views.says: A bridge should bend a little. The roots sway and spring back, and they grow thicker where they are pushed.

views.who: Gayathri, who designs buildings for places with earthquakes
views.says: Bending a little is safer than being stiff. A building that can sway in an earthquake bends instead of snapping.

items.ask: Should a bridge bend or be stiff? Pick a side and give evidence from this unit. Then answer back from another side.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side with evidence, for example that bamboo bends in a storm and springs back, or that a stiff ruler on its edge hardly sags. It then answers back, for example that too much bending can crack metal, or that a stiff thing that cannot bend may snap. The best answers say it depends on the material and the job.
items.why: Both are true in different places. Steel bridges are stiff but allowed to move a little at their joints. Root bridges and tall buildings in earthquake zones are safer because they can bend.

items.p: In the story, Iba tied the young roots tightly so the storm couldn't move them. The loose roots, thrashed by the wind, grew thicker. Why do you think the tied roots stayed thin?
items.a: A strong answer says that the loose roots were bent and pulled by the wind every day, and a living root answers those forces by growing thicker, stronger wood. The tied roots felt no bending, so they had nothing to answer. It may link this to swaying trees or to bones that grow stronger with exercise.
items.why: Living beings reshape their bodies to match the forces on them. Trees, roots and bones all grow stronger where they are pushed and pulled.
items.context: In this unit's story, Iba helps her aunt grow a living root bridge in Meghalaya. She ties the young roots so they can't move, while some loose roots are thrashed by the wind.

items.p: Draw how the Himalayas were made. First draw India's plate moving north towards Asia, with an arrow for the push. Then draw the rock between them after the push, folded up into mountains.
items.a: A strong drawing shows two blocks of land with flat layers of rock between them, and an arrow pushing one block towards the other. The second picture shows the layers crumpled and folded upwards, like a towel pushed against a wall.
items.why: A slow, huge push changes the shape of rock, just as a hand changes the shape of dough. The Himalayas are still being pushed up today.

items.p: Many people think a moving thing needs a push all the time to keep moving. Aristotle, a thinker in ancient Greece, thought so too. Plan a test with a marble to check this idea.
items.a: A strong answer rolls the same marble with the same push on carpet, on a tiled floor, and on a smooth steel plate or tray. It measures how far the marble goes each time. If the marble goes further on smoother surfaces, then something on the surface was slowing it. With nothing slowing it, it would not need a push to keep going.
items.why: Galileo did tests like this in the early 1600s. He showed that moving things keep moving unless a force, like friction, slows them down.

items.p: Bend a steel paper clip back and forth quickly, 20 times, in the same place. Then touch the bend gently. Predict what you will feel, and what will happen if you keep going. Explain why.
items.a: A strong answer predicts that the bend feels warm, and that after more bends the clip snaps. Each bend pushes rows of atoms past each other, and that movement turns into heat. After many bends, tiny cracks grow until the clip breaks.
items.why: Squeezing and bending something over and over warms it up. The same thing heats the inside of Jupiter's moon Io, which has more volcanoes than anywhere else we know.

experiments.title: The Clay Drop Test
experiments.question: Does dropping clay from higher up squash it more?
experiments.predict: Before you drop anything, guess. Will the clay dropped from 80 cm be more squashed, less squashed, or the same as from 10 cm? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Change only the height. Use four clay balls of the same size, made of the same clay. Drop each onto the same steel plate. Let go, don't throw.

materials.item: modelling clay or firm chapati dough, enough for four lemon-sized balls
a steel plate or a tile
a 30 cm ruler and a measuring tape
a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: Guess, drop clay from four heights, measure the flat patches, and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar chart, with one bar for each height. Make each bar as tall as that patch was wide.

setup.art: A child rolling a lemon-sized ball of clay between two palms, with three more equal balls on a plate.
setup.caption: 1. Make four clay balls, all the same size.

setup.art: A ruler standing upright on a steel plate, a hand holding a clay ball level with the 10 cm mark.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a ball beside the ruler, 10 cm above the plate. Let go. Don't throw.

setup.art: A clay ball with a flat bottom on its side, a small ruler measuring across the flat patch.
setup.caption: 3. Measure how wide the flat patch is.

setup.art: Four squashed clay balls in a row, the flat patches getting wider from left to right, labels 10, 20, 40, 80 cm.
setup.caption: 4. Repeat from 20, 40 and 80 cm. Compare the patches.

flow.do: 1. Make four clay balls the same size. Roll all the clay into one long sausage and cut it into four equal pieces. 2. Roll each one smooth between your palms.
flow.say: We need four balls exactly the same size. Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Make four clay balls. Make them all the same size. Roll them smooth.

ask.q: Why must the balls be the same size?
good: So it's a fair test.
So only the height is different.

flow.context: This is the first step of the clay drop test. You find out whether a higher drop squashes clay more.

flow.do: 1. Put the plate on the floor. 2. Hold the measuring tape upright beside it. 3. Ask your child to guess which drop will squash most.
flow.say: We'll drop from 10, 20, 40 and 80 centimetres. Which one will squash most? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the plate on the floor. Hold a tape upright beside it. Guess. Which drop will squash most?

flow.do: 1. Hold the first ball beside the tape, its bottom level with 10 cm. 2. Let go without pushing. 3. Measure the width of the flat patch with the ruler. 4. Repeat with a new ball from 20, 40 and 80 cm.
flow.say: Let go gently, don't throw. Now let's measure the flat part on the bottom.
flow.kid: Hold the ball at 10 cm. Let go. Don't throw! Measure the flat patch. Do the same from 20, 40 and 80 cm.
flow.parent: Measure straight across the widest part of the flat patch. If the patch is not round, measure the longest way and keep to that each time.

flow.do: Help your child draw a bar chart of the patch widths, one bar for each height.
flow.say: Let's turn the numbers into a picture. One bar for each height. The taller the bar, the more squashed the ball.
flow.kid: Draw one bar for each height. Make it as tall as the patch was wide. Do the bars grow?

check.q: In the clay drop chart, the bars get taller as the height goes up. This means…
options: Higher drops squash the clay more
Higher drops squash the clay less
check.why: Higher drops squash the clay more. Each bar is the width of a flat patch, so taller means more squashed. Picking 'less' usually means the bars were read the wrong way round.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how wide the flat patch was after each drop
chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. Does a higher drop squash clay more? What did you measure that shows it? Why do you think it happens?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think now. What you measured. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: dropping clay from higher squashes it more. What I saw: the patch was 1 cm wide from 10 cm, but 4 cm wide from 80 cm. Why: from higher up the ball is going faster, so the plate has to push harder to stop it. A bigger push makes a bigger squash.

experiments.context: This is the clay drop test. You drop equal clay balls onto a plate from different heights. Then you measure the flat patch on the bottom, to see how squashed each one got.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how wide the flat patch was after each drop
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what results can look like. Your numbers will be different.

experiments.title: Squash, Spring Back or Break?
experiments.question: When the same force hits different materials, what does each one do?
experiments.predict: Before testing, guess for each thing. Will it stay changed, spring back, or break? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Give every thing the same force. Use the same ball, dropped down the same paper tube, from the same height. Use pieces of about the same size.
results_table: Stays changed, springs back or breaks?

materials.item: a biscuit, a lump of chapati dough, a slice of raw potato, a piece of boiled potato, a kitchen sponge, and a small stone from a plant pot
a sheet of newspaper rolled into a tube about 40 cm tall
a cricket ball, or another heavy ball about the same size
steel plates or tiles, one for each thing

experiments.safety: A heavy ball can chip a tile or hurt toes. Keep feet away, and let a grown-up hold the tube steady. Eat nothing that has been tested.

schedule.what: Guess, then drop the ball onto six things, and sort them.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw the six things in three groups: stays changed, springs back, breaks.

setup.art: A table with a biscuit, a lump of chapati dough, a slice of raw potato, a piece of boiled potato, a kitchen sponge and a stone, each on its own steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Set out six things on plates.

setup.art: A tube of rolled newspaper standing upright on a biscuit, a hand dropping a cricket ball into the top.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the paper tube on one thing. Drop the ball down the tube.

setup.art: Three groups on the table labelled STAYS CHANGED, SPRINGS BACK, BREAKS, with the tested things sorted into them.
setup.caption: 3. Sort each thing: stays changed, springs back, or breaks.

flow.do: 1. Put each of the six things on a plate. 2. Ask your child to press each one gently with a finger first.
flow.say: Feel each one with your finger. Which do you think will squash? Which will spring back? Which will break?
flow.kid: Press each thing gently with a finger. Then guess. Squash, spring back, or break? Write your guesses.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Squash, Spring Back or Break test. You drop a heavy ball onto six different things.

flow.do: 1. Roll the newspaper into a tube just wide enough for the ball. 2. Stand it upright on the first thing. 3. Drop the ball into the top. 4. Lift the tube and look. 5. Write what happened. 6. Repeat for each thing.
flow.say: Same ball, same tube, same height every time. Now what happened? Was your guess right?
flow.kid: Stand the tube on one thing. Drop the ball in the top. Lift the tube. What happened? Write it down.
flow.parent: Expect: the biscuit breaks. The dough and boiled potato stay squashed. The sponge springs back. The raw potato may dent a little or crack. The stone does not change at all that you can see. That is a useful result, not a failure.

flow.do: Sort the six things into three groups on the table.
flow.say: Let's sort them. Stays changed. Springs back. Breaks. Where does the stone go?
flow.kid: Sort the six things into three groups. Stays changed. Springs back. Breaks. Where does the stone go?

ask.q: The stone didn't change. Did the force do nothing to it?
good: It changed a tiny bit, too little to see.
It sprang back straight away.
Stone needs a much bigger force to change.

check.q: The sponge squashed, then sprang back. A word for this is…
check.why: Elastic means it springs back. Picking 'plastic' mixes it up with dough, which stays changed. Picking 'brittle' means breaking, and the sponge did not break.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. Do different things react to the same push in different ways? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think now. What you saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: different materials react to the same force in different ways. What I saw: the biscuit broke, the dough stayed squashed, and the sponge sprang back. Why: the tiny parts inside are held together differently. In dough they slide, in a sponge the thin walls spring back, and in a biscuit they crack apart.

experiments.context: This is a drop test. You drop the same heavy ball onto six different things, like a biscuit, dough and a sponge. Then you sort them by what they did.

experiments.title: Wet Ball Prints: catching a bounce
experiments.question: Does a bouncing ball really squash? Does a higher drop squash it more?
experiments.predict: Before you test, guess. Will the wet circle from shoulder height be bigger, smaller, or the same as from knee height? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same ball, wet the same way each time, on the same kind of paper. Change only the drop height. Do each height 3 times, because one try can be a fluke. Then put the three widths in order and take the middle one.

materials.item: a tennis ball (best, because its fuzz holds water), or a rubber ball
a shallow bowl of water
sheets of newspaper or brown paper, where a wet circle shows up darker
a ruler and a pencil

schedule.what: Drop a wet ball from three heights, measure the prints, and compare.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three biggest wet circles, side by side.

setup.art: A rubber ball being dipped bottom-first into a shallow bowl of water.
setup.caption: 1. Dip the bottom half of the ball in water.

setup.art: A child holding the wet ball at knee height above a sheet of dark paper on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Drop it from knee height onto the paper.

setup.art: A sheet of dark paper with three wet circles of growing size, labelled knee, waist, shoulder.
setup.caption: 3. Repeat from waist and shoulder height. Draw round each wet circle and measure it.

flow.do: 1. Lay paper on the floor. 2. Wet the bottom of the ball and set it down gently on the paper. 3. Lift it straight up and look at the small wet dot it made. 4. Draw round the dot with a pencil before it dries.
flow.say: When this ball just sits on the floor, how much of it touches? Look, only a small dot. Now let's see how much touches when it bounces.
flow.kid: Wet the ball. Set it down gently on the paper. Lift it. See the small dot? Now let's try a bounce.
flow.context: This is the first step of the wet ball prints test. You catch the shape of a bounce with a wet ball.

flow.do: 1. Dip the bottom half of the ball in water and shake off the drips. 2. Drop it from knee height onto a dry part of the paper. 3. Catch it after one bounce, so it doesn't print twice. 4. Draw round the wet circle with a pencil straight away, before it dries. 5. Measure across the pencil circle. 6. Do steps 1 to 5 three times from knee height, then three times from waist height, then three times from shoulder height. Wet the ball again each time.
flow.say: Look at the wet circle. Is it bigger or smaller than the dot? Now let's try from higher.
flow.kid: Dip the ball in water. Shake off the drips. Drop it from your knee. Catch it after one bounce. Draw round the wet circle and measure it. Now try waist and shoulder height.
flow.parent: The wet circle is clearly bigger than the dot the ball made resting on the paper. That shows the ball squashed flatter for a moment. A tennis ball works best, because its fuzz holds water. A smooth rubber ball can leave a patchy print, so wipe it all over with a wet cloth instead of dipping it. The prints dry fast, so draw round them at once. If a circle is hard to see, look at the paper from a slant, against the light. The circles from the three heights differ by only a few millimetres, so some of your results may be close or in a different order. That is an honest result. Look at the average of the three tries, not one.

flow.do: For each height, put the three widths in order and write the middle one in the last column. Put the three middle values side by side. Then drop a ball of dough from waist height onto a clean sheet of paper, for comparison.
flow.say: Which height made the biggest circle? Now let's drop a ball of dough from waist height. What do you think it will do?
flow.kid: Which circle is biggest? Now drop a ball of dough. Does it bounce? Why not?

check.q: Why doesn't the dough ball bounce?
options: It stays squashed, so nothing pushes it back up
The floor doesn't push on it
check.why: It stays squashed, so nothing pushes it back up. Picking 'too light' links bouncing with weight, but light balls bounce well. Picking 'the floor doesn't push' is not right either: the floor pushed hard enough to flatten it.

chart.title: Made-up example results: how wide the wet ball print was
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

flow.do: Ask your child what a bounce is. Wait for their idea before saying anything.
flow.say: Resting, the ball touched only a small dot. In the bounce, the wet circle was much bigger. What happened to the ball when it hit the floor? What sent it back up?
flow.kid: The bounce made a much bigger circle than the dot. What happened to the ball? What sent it back up?
flow.think: Tennis players' rackets also squash when they hit the ball. Why might that help?
flow.parent: A good answer: the floor pushed up and squashed the ball flatter for a moment. Then the ball sprang back to round, pushing on the floor, and the floor pushed it back up. One push changed both its shape and its direction.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. Does a bouncing ball squash? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happens?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think now. What you saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a bouncing ball squashes, and it squashes more from higher up. What I saw: the wet circle was about 3.5 cm across from knee height and 4.5 cm from shoulder height. Both were much bigger than the 1 cm dot when it rested. Why: from higher it hits faster, so the floor pushes harder and squashes it flatter. Then it springs back up.

experiments.context: This is the wet ball prints test. You wet the bottom of a ball and drop it on paper. The wet circle shows how flat the ball squashed during the bounce.

activities.title: Shape the Dough

materials.item: a ball of chapati dough or play dough, about the size of an orange
a rolling pin

schedule.what: Change the dough's shape with every kind of force, and play the shape dance.

activities.record: Draw the dough after each force. Label it squash, stretch, twist or bend.

setup.art: A child's hands pressing an orange-sized ball of chapati dough flat on a board.
setup.caption: 1. Squash the dough flat.

setup.art: Hands pulling a dough snake longer, and then twisting the snake like a rope.
setup.caption: 2. Roll a snake. Stretch it. Twist it.

setup.art: A dough snake bent into a horseshoe, and a kitchen sponge squeezed in a fist beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Bend it. Then squeeze a sponge and compare.

flow.do: Clap a slow beat. On each clap, call out a shape. Your child makes it with their body. Squash means curl up small. Stretch means reach tall. Twist means turn the top half while the feet stay still. Bend means touch the toes.
flow.say: Squash! Stretch! Twist! Bend! Now, spring back! Now, stay like clay!
flow.kid: Listen for the claps. Squash, curl up small. Stretch, reach tall. Twist your top half. Bend down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Shape the Dough. You warm up with a shape dance, then change the shape of dough with forces.

flow.do: Give your child the dough. 1. Squash it flat into a chapati. 2. Roll it into a long snake. 3. Stretch the snake. 4. Twist it like a rope. 5. Bend it into a horseshoe. 6. Press a thumb in to make a diya.
flow.say: Which force did you use? Push or pull? When you stopped, did the dough stay in its new shape?
flow.kid: Squash the dough flat. Roll a snake. Stretch it. Twist it. Bend it. Press your thumb in. Does it stay changed?

ask.q: Did the dough spring back after each force?
good: No, it stayed in its new shape.
It kept the shape I made.

flow.do: Now squeeze a sponge or a rubber ball and let go. Compare it with the dough.
flow.say: Dough stays changed. Scientists call that a plastic change. The sponge springs back. That's called elastic. Which is better for making a diya?
flow.kid: Squeeze a sponge. Let go. It springs back! Dough stays changed. Which one is better for making a diya?

check.q: Dough keeps its new shape after you squash it. Scientists call this…
check.why: A plastic change means it stays changed. Picking 'elastic' means springing back, which is what a sponge does. Picking 'brittle' means breaking, like a biscuit.

flow.think: Why is it useful that chapati dough stays flat after you roll it?

activities.context: In this activity you change the shape of a ball of dough in every way you can: squash, stretch, twist and bend. Then you compare it with a springy sponge.

activities.title: The Bendy Sponge and the Standing Ruler

materials.item: a long kitchen sponge or a piece of foam
a marker pen
a 30 cm plastic ruler
two tins or two stacks of books the same height, and a small book

activities.safety: Press gently on the ruler. A snapped plastic ruler can have sharp edges.

schedule.what: Bend a lined sponge, then press a ruler flat and on its edge.

activities.record: Draw the bent sponge and its lines. Write which way the ruler bent less.

setup.art: A long kitchen sponge with five straight lines drawn down its thin side in marker, from the top face to the bottom face.
setup.caption: 1. Draw straight lines across the thin side of a long sponge.

setup.art: Two hands bending the sponge into a curve: the lines are squeezed together on the inside and spread apart on the outside.
setup.caption: 2. Bend it. Look at the inside and the outside of the bend.

setup.art: A plastic ruler lying flat across two tins, sagging under a book, and the same ruler standing on its edge, held by its ends, hardly bending under a finger.
setup.caption: 3. Press the middle of a ruler, flat and then on its edge.

flow.do: Draw five straight lines from top to bottom on the thin side of the sponge, each about two fingers apart.
flow.say: Let's draw lines on this sponge, so we can see what happens inside it when it bends.
flow.kid: Turn the sponge on its side. Draw five straight lines from top to bottom. Leave two fingers between them.
flow.context: This is the first step of the bendy sponge activity. You find out what happens inside a bend.

flow.do: Bend the sponge into a curve, with the lined side facing you. Look at the lines on the inside of the curve, then on the outside.
flow.say: Look at the inside of the bend. What happened to the lines? Now the outside?
flow.kid: Bend the sponge. Look inside the curve. Are the lines closer? Now look outside. Are they further apart?

good: The inside got squashed and the lines got closer.
The outside got stretched and the lines spread apart.

check.q: When something bends, its inside curve is…
check.why: Squashed. The lines on the inside crowd together. Picking 'stretched' swaps the two sides: the outside is the stretched part.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler flat across the two tins. 2. Put the small book on its middle and watch it sag. 3. Take the book off. Stand the ruler on its thin edge across the tins. Your child steadies it with one hand. 4. Your child presses the middle down with one finger.
flow.say: Same ruler. Lying flat, it sags under the book. On its edge, push it with your finger. Does it bend? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lay the ruler flat on two tins. Put a book on it. It sags! Now stand it on its edge. Press its middle with one finger.
flow.parent: A book will not balance on the thin edge, so your child presses with a finger instead. A plastic ruler on its edge may tip sideways, so steady it. On its edge, the top and bottom of the ruler are far apart. To bend, the top must squash a lot and the bottom must stretch a lot. So it resists. This is why steel beams have an I shape, and why bamboo, a hollow tube, is so stiff.

flow.do: Look around the home for tubes, rods and bars: a broom handle, a curtain rod, a steel pipe, a bamboo stick.
flow.say: Can you spot tubes and pipes near us? Hollow tubes are hard to bend for how light they are.
flow.kid: Look for tubes, pipes and sticks. A tube is hard to bend. Can you find one?
flow.think: Your leg bones are tubes too. Why might a tube be a good shape for a bone?

activities.context: In this activity you draw lines on a sponge and bend it to see what happens inside a bend. Then you find out why a ruler on its edge hardly bends.

activities.title: Wring It, Twist It, Make a Rope

materials.item: a small towel and a bucket of water
cotton wool, the kind used for diya wicks or first aid: two equal tufts, each about the size of a lime
a strip of paper with lines drawn across it
a small plastic bag with handles, and about 20 coins

schedule.what: Wring a towel, twist a lined strip, and twist cotton wool into a wick that holds coins.

activities.record: Write how many coins the loose strand held, and how many the twisted wick held.

setup.art: Two small hands wringing a wet towel over a bucket, water dripping.
setup.caption: 1. Wring a wet towel.

setup.art: A paper strip with straight lines across it, twisted so the lines become slanting spirals.
setup.caption: 2. Twist a lined paper strip. Watch the lines.

setup.art: A pinch of cotton wool twisted into a wick, held up by a child's fingers, with a small plastic bag of coins hanging from its lower end.
setup.caption: 3. Twist cotton wool into a wick. Hang a bag of coins from it.

flow.do: 1. Soak the towel and lift it out. 2. Your child wrings it out over the bucket, hands turning opposite ways.
flow.say: Twist it tighter and tighter. What happens to the water? Why?
flow.kid: Wring the wet towel. Turn your hands opposite ways. Where does the water go?

ask.q: Why does twisting push the water out?
good: The twist squeezes the cloth tighter.
The cloth gets squashed so water has no room.

flow.context: This is the first step of the twisting activity. You wring a towel, then twist cotton wool into a strong wick.

flow.do: 1. Hold the lined paper strip at both ends. 2. Twist one end while the other stays still. 3. Watch the lines.
flow.say: What happened to the straight lines? They turned into spirals. That's what a twist looks like.
flow.kid: Hold the paper strip at both ends. Twist one end. What happens to the lines?

flow.do: 1. Pull one tuft into a loose strand as long as your hand. Don't twist it. 2. Hold its ends and pull gently. 3. Pull the second tuft into a strand of the same length. 4. Hold one end still, and twist the other end round and round about 30 times. Keep the strand pulled straight while you twist. 5. Hold the two ends together and let the middle hang down. It twists round itself into a strong cord, with a loop at the bottom. 6. Hook the bag handles through the loop. Hold the two top ends tightly and add coins one at a time.
flow.say: The loose strand pulls apart easily. Now the wick, made from the same amount of cotton. How many coins will it hold? Why?
flow.kid: Pull the loose cotton gently. It comes apart! Now twist the same amount of cotton round and round. Hold its two ends together and let it twist into a cord. Hang the bag on the loop. Add coins.
flow.parent: Try hanging the empty bag from the loose strand too. It usually pulls apart at once. The twisted cord should hold many coins. Folding it makes two twisted strands wind round each other, like a real rope, and the loop means no knot is needed. How many coins it holds depends on the cotton and how tightly you twist. Even a few coins, when the loose strand holds none, is a clear result. If the bag fills before it breaks, that is a good result too. The twist squeezes the short fibres against each other. Friction, the grip between them, makes them share the pull. Cotton thread and coir rope are made this way.

check.q: The twisted wick holds more than the loose strand because…
options: The twist squeezes the fibres, so they grip each other and share the pull
The fibres are stuck with glue
check.why: The twist squeezes the fibres so they grip each other and share the pull. Picking 'longer fibres' is a good guess, but each fibre stays the same length. There is no glue at all.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. Does twisting make cotton stronger? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think it happens?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think now. What you saw. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: twisting cotton makes it much stronger. What I saw: the loose strand pulled apart, but the twisted wick held several coins. Why: the twist squeezes the fibres together, so they grip each other and share the pull.

activities.context: In this activity you wring a wet towel, twist a lined paper strip, and twist cotton wool into a wick that can hold a bag of coins. It shows what a twist does.

activities.title: The Spaghetti Puzzle

materials.item: a handful of dry spaghetti or long dry noodles
a large paper bag or a towel to catch flying bits

activities.safety: Bend the spaghetti inside a bag or under a towel, and keep it away from eyes. Small sharp bits can fly.

schedule.what: Snap spaghetti, count the pieces, then try the twist trick.

activities.record: Write how many pieces each stick broke into. Draw the best break.

setup.art: Two hands holding the ends of a stick of dry spaghetti inside an open paper bag, bending it into a curve.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the spaghetti by its ends, inside a bag. Bend it slowly.

setup.art: Three or four pieces of broken spaghetti lying on a towel, with a tally chart beside them.
setup.caption: 2. Count the pieces. Do it 5 times.

setup.art: Hands twisting a stick of spaghetti about three-quarters of a turn before bending it.
setup.caption: 3. Now twist it about three-quarters of a turn first, then bend it slowly.

flow.do: 1. Hold a stick of spaghetti by both ends, inside the bag. 2. Bend it slowly until it snaps. 3. Count the pieces. 4. Do this 5 times.
flow.say: Guess first. How many pieces will it break into? Let's count.
flow.kid: Guess how many pieces. Hold the spaghetti by both ends, inside the bag. Bend it till it snaps. Count!
flow.context: This is the first step of the spaghetti puzzle. You try to snap dry spaghetti into just two pieces.

flow.do: Ask your child why it never broke into just two pieces. Listen to their idea first. Then tell the story of the puzzle.
flow.say: Why do you think it breaks into three or more? A famous scientist, Richard Feynman, tried for a whole evening and never got two. In 2005, two French scientists explained why. When it first snaps, both halves spring back so fast that they snap again.
flow.kid: Why do you think it breaks into many pieces? A famous scientist tried this all evening. He never got two pieces! When it snaps, the halves spring back so fast they snap again.

check.q: Why does dry spaghetti usually break into 3 or more pieces?
options: The first snap makes the halves spring back so fast they break again
Spaghetti is made of three pieces stuck together
check.why: The first snap makes the halves spring back so fast that they break again. Picking 'slipping hands' is a fair worry, but it happens even with a machine. Spaghetti is one solid piece, not three stuck together.

flow.do: Try the trick found at MIT in 2018. Hold both ends and twist the spaghetti about three-quarters of a turn. Then bend it slowly.
flow.say: Scientists found a twist can change how a bend breaks. Can we get two pieces? It's hard. They used a machine.
flow.kid: Now twist it about three-quarters of a turn. Then bend it slowly. Two pieces? It's tricky. Keep trying!
flow.parent: This trick is hard by hand. The scientists twisted the spaghetti about three-quarters of a turn or more before bending it, and used a machine to bend it slowly. If it doesn't work, that's fine. The point is that twisting changes how something breaks.
flow.think: Scientists solved this puzzle only in 2005. What other kitchen puzzles might nobody have solved yet?

activities.context: This is a kitchen puzzle. You bend dry spaghetti until it snaps, and count the pieces. Scientists only explained the result in 2005.

activities.title: Is the Table Bending? (a laser and a mirror)

materials.item: a small flat mirror, like a make-up mirror
a low-power laser pointer, used only by a grown-up
a table near a wall, and a strip of tape for the wall

activities.safety: Only a grown-up holds the laser. Never point it at anyone's eyes, and never look into the beam or its reflection. Use a toy-strength laser pointer.

schedule.what: Show that a table bends when you press it, using a laser beam bounced off a mirror.

activities.record: Draw the table, the mirror, the beam and the dot on the wall. Mark how far the dot moved.

setup.art: A small mirror lying flat in the middle of a wooden table near a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a mirror flat on the middle of a table.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a laser pointer still, its beam bouncing off the mirror to a red dot on the wall.
setup.caption: 2. A grown-up shines a laser onto the mirror. Find the dot on the wall.

setup.art: A child pressing down gently on the table, a hand-width from the mirror, while the red dot on the wall moves a little from a tape mark.
setup.caption: 3. Press the table firmly next to the mirror. Watch the dot move.

flow.do: 1. Lay the mirror flat in the middle of a table that is at least 2 metres from a wall. 2. A grown-up props the laser on books on a chair beside the table. Keep it off the table, so pressing the table cannot move it. 3. Aim it at the mirror and find the red dot on the wall. 4. Stick a strip of tape on the wall, with its edge exactly at the dot.
flow.say: Does a solid table change shape when you press it? We can't see it. Let's use a beam of light to find out.
flow.kid: Does a hard table change shape when you press it? Ask a grown-up to set up the laser. Find the dot on the wall.
flow.context: This is the first step of the laser and mirror activity. You find out whether a hard table bends when you press it.
flow.parent: No laser pointer at home? They are cheap at stationery and electronics shops. If you don't have one, skip this activity. The wet ball prints test shows a hidden squash too.

flow.do: Your child presses down firmly with both hands on the table, a hand-width away from the mirror, then lets go. Everyone watches the dot against the edge of the tape.
flow.say: Press down. Watch the dot. Now press harder. What happens?
flow.kid: Press the table next to the mirror with both hands. Watch the dot. Did it move? Now press a bit harder.
flow.parent: The table bends a tiny bit, which tilts the mirror. The long beam to the wall turns that tiny tilt into a movement of the dot, usually only a millimetre or two. Look closely at the tape edge. A harder press moves it more. If you can't see it move, use a wall further away, or let a grown-up lean on the table. A wooden table bends more than a stone or steel one. If the dot still does not move, that does not show the table stayed still. It only means the bend was too small for this set-up.

check.q: Why did the dot move when you pressed the table?
options: The table bent a tiny bit and tilted the mirror
check.why: The table bent a tiny bit and tilted the mirror. Picking 'the laser moved' is sensible, which is why it rests on a chair, not on the table. The wall did not move, as the tape mark shows.

flow.do: Talk about what this means.
flow.say: Even hard things change shape when pushed. Steel bridges sag when trucks cross. Tall buildings sway in the wind. The change is just too small to see.
flow.kid: Even a hard table bends a tiny bit. So do bridges and buildings. It's just too small to see!
flow.think: If even a table bends, does the floor bend when you stand on it?

activities.context: In this activity a grown-up bounces a laser beam off a mirror on a table. When you press the table, the dot on the wall moves. It shows that even hard things change shape.

activities.title: Make Mountains, Squash a Planet

materials.item: a towel or a dupatta, and a smooth floor
two strips of paper, about 2 fingers wide and as long as your arm
a pencil and sticky tape

activities.safety: Keep the sharp pencil tip pointing down, away from faces.

schedule.what: Fold a towel into mountains, then spin paper rings into a squashed planet.

activities.record: Draw the folded towel as mountains. Draw the paper rings before and while spinning.

setup.art: A towel laid flat on the floor, a child's hands pushing one end towards a wall.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a towel flat. Push one end towards a wall.

setup.art: The towel crumpled into ridges and folds against the wall, like a mountain range, with a small toy shell on top.
setup.caption: 2. Watch it fold up into 'mountains'.

setup.art: Two crossed paper rings taped to a pencil at the bottom and loose at the top, squashing into a flat oval as the pencil spins between palms.
setup.caption: 3. Spin the paper rings on a pencil. Watch them squash.

flow.do: 1. Lay the towel flat on the floor, one end against a wall. 2. Put a small object, like a toy shell or a button, on the towel. 3. Your child pushes the other end slowly towards the wall.
flow.say: This towel is the old sea floor. The wall is Asia. You are India, pushing north. Watch what happens.
flow.kid: The towel is the sea floor. The wall is Asia. You are India. Push slowly towards the wall!

ask.q: What happened to the towel? Where did the shell go?
good: It folded up into hills.
The shell got lifted up high.

flow.context: This is the first step of Make Mountains. You act out how India pushing into Asia folded up the Himalayas.

flow.do: Talk about the real Himalayas.
flow.say: India's plate moves north about 5 centimetres every year. About 50 million years ago it began to crash into Asia. The rock folded up like the towel. That's why sea shells are found high in the Himalayas.
flow.kid: India still moves north, about as fast as fingernails grow. It folded up the Himalayas. Sea shells are found on top!

check.q: Why are fossil sea shells found high in the Himalayas?
options: The old sea floor was pushed up into mountains
The sea was once higher than the mountains
check.why: The old sea floor was pushed up into mountains. Picking 'the sea was once higher' is a natural guess, but it was the land that rose. Birds could not carry whole layers of rock full of shells.

flow.do: 1. Make each paper strip into a ring. 2. Cross the two rings at right angles, like the lines on a globe. 3. Tape both rings to the pencil at the bottom. At the top, tape them together and push the pencil up through a small hole, so they can slide. 4. Spin the pencil fast between your palms.
flow.say: This is the Earth. Spin it fast. What happens to its shape?
flow.kid: Make a paper globe on a pencil. Spin the pencil fast between your hands. What happens to the shape?
flow.parent: As the rings spin, they flatten at the top and bottom and bulge at the middle. The real Earth spins too. It is about 43 kilometres wider across the equator than from pole to pole. The top of the rings must be free to slide down the pencil, or they can't flatten. If the rings hardly change, spin faster, or use thinner paper. The change is small, just as the real Earth is only a little squashed. A small bulge is a fair result.

chart.title: How wide the Earth is, measured two ways

data.label: Pole to pole, through the middle
Across the equator, through the middle

chart.note: The difference is about 43 kilometres. The bars look nearly the same, because 43 is tiny next to 12,700.

flow.think: The spinning Earth is squashed. Is anything in space a perfect ball?

activities.context: In this activity you push a towel into folds to see how the Himalayas were made. Then you spin paper rings on a pencil to see how the spinning Earth bulges.

projects.title: Am I Taller in the Morning?

materials.item: a measuring tape and a strip of paper taped upright to a wall
a hardback book, to rest flat on the head
a pencil and the results table

schedule.what: Set up the wall strip. Measure at bedtime. Guess what the morning will show.
Measure as soon as you wake up, and again at bedtime.
Measure first thing in the morning, find the differences, and talk about astronauts' bones.

projects.record: Fill in the table: day, morning height, bedtime height, difference. Draw the two heights as two bars.

setup.art: A strip of paper taped upright on a wall, a child standing barefoot against it with heels touching the wall.
setup.caption: 1. Stand barefoot, heels against the wall.

setup.art: A grown-up resting a hardback book flat on the child's head and marking the wall strip with a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Rest a book flat on the head. Mark the strip under it.

setup.art: The wall strip with two pencil marks very close together, labelled MORNING and NIGHT, and a ruler measuring the gap.
setup.caption: 3. Measure morning and night. Find the gap.

flow.do: 1. Tape a paper strip upright on the wall. 2. Your child stands barefoot, heels, back and head against the wall. 3. Rest a book flat on their head and mark the strip under it. 4. Measure the height from the floor.
flow.say: Let's measure you tonight. Tomorrow morning we'll measure again. Do you think you'll be the same?
flow.kid: Stand against the wall. Heels back. Stand tall. A grown-up marks your height. Will you be the same in the morning?
flow.context: This is the first step of the morning and night project. You measure your height at bedtime and as soon as you wake up.

flow.do: Measure again as soon as your child wakes up, before they walk around much. Use the same wall, book and way of standing.
flow.say: Straight out of bed. Same way, same book. Let's see.
flow.kid: Just woken up? Go straight to the wall. Stand the same way. Measure!
flow.wait: Measure first thing the next morning.

flow.do: At bedtime on day 2, measure again in the same way. First thing on the morning of day 3, measure once more. Write every number in the table.
flow.say: Two nights, two tries, because one try can be a fluke.
flow.kid: Measure at bedtime tonight. Measure again first thing tomorrow morning. Write each number in the table.
flow.wait: Measure at bedtime on day 2, and first thing on day 3.

flow.do: Find the difference between each bedtime and the next morning. Then talk about why.
flow.say: You were taller in the morning! During the day, your weight squashes the soft pads between the bones of your back. At night, lying down, they spring back.
flow.kid: Were you taller in the morning? Your back squashes a little during the day. At night it springs back!

check.q: Why are you a little taller in the morning?
options: The pads in your spine spring back while you lie down at night
Bones grow every night by 1 cm
check.why: The soft pads in your spine spring back while you lie down. Picking 'bones grow 1 cm a night' would make you more than 3 metres taller in a year. The wall did not move.

flow.do: Talk about astronauts.
flow.say: In space, astronauts float, so nothing squashes their spine. They grow a few centimetres taller. But their bones get weaker, because nothing pushes on them. So they exercise for about two hours every day.
flow.kid: In space, astronauts grow a little taller! But their bones get weaker, because nothing pushes on them. So they exercise every day.
flow.think: Your bones get stronger when you run and jump. What could you do today that your bones would like?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences. First, what I think. Second, what I saw. Third, why I think it happened.
flow.say: Tell me three things. Are you taller in the morning? What did you measure that shows it? Why do you think it happens?
flow.kid: Say or write three things. What you think now. What you measured. Why it happened.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. Any honest answer with all three parts is good. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: I am a little taller in the morning than at night. What I saw: I was 130 cm in the morning and 129 cm at bedtime. Why: my weight squashes the soft pads in my back during the day. They spring back when I lie down.

projects.context: In this 3-day project you measure your height at bedtime and again as soon as you wake up. You find out that your own body changes shape every day.

challenges.title: The Paper Bridge
challenges.problem: Make one sheet of paper hold as many coins as possible over a gap between two books 15 cm apart.
constraints: Use only one sheet of A4 paper.
You may fold, roll or cut it, but you may not use tape or glue.
The coins sit in the middle of the gap. The bridge fails when it sags down to the table.
materials: one sheet of A4 paper for each try
two books of the same thickness
general: Fold the paper like a fan, so each fold is a little wall standing on its edge.
Roll it into tubes, and lay the tubes side by side.
Fold the two long edges up, like a gutter, so the sides stand up.
creative: Make a fan, then lay a flat strip on top so the coins have a floor.
Make an arch under the bridge, pressing its feet against the books.
Copy the wavy layer inside a cardboard box.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own shape. Draw it, test it and count the coins. Can you beat the fan?

setup.art: Two books 15 cm apart with a flat sheet of paper across the gap, sagging under one coin.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a flat sheet across the gap. Add coins until it sags.

setup.art: The same sheet folded into a zigzag fan lying across the gap, with a stack of coins on top.
setup.caption: 2. Fold a new sheet like a fan. Test again.

setup.art: A row of paper tubes and a gutter shape lined up next to a tally of coins for each.
setup.caption: 3. Try tubes and other shapes. Count the coins each time.

flow.do: 1. Put the two books 15 cm apart. 2. Lay a flat sheet across them. 3. Add coins one at a time to the middle until it sags to the table. 4. Write the number.
flow.say: Let's see how many coins a flat sheet can hold. Guess first.
flow.kid: Put two books 15 cm apart. Lay a flat sheet across. Add coins one by one. How many before it sags?
flow.context: This is the first step of the paper bridge challenge. You find out how strong a flat sheet of paper is.

flow.do: Before trying anything, draw three ideas together.
flow.say: Engineers design before they build. Can we make the paper stronger just by changing its shape?
flow.kid: Think like an engineer. Draw three shapes that might be stronger. Do this before you build.

flow.do: 1. Build and test each idea with a new sheet. 2. Count the coins each time. 3. Write the numbers.
flow.say: Test each shape the same way. Which holds the most?
flow.kid: Build each shape. Test it. Count the coins. Which is strongest?
flow.parent: A fan folded with many narrow folds usually holds the most. Tubes do well too. The same amount of paper becomes many times stronger, just by changing its shape. That is why tin roofs are wavy and cardboard has a wavy middle.

chart.title: Made-up example results: coins held by one sheet of paper
chart.y: Coins held before it sagged to the table
chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

check.q: Why does the folded fan hold more coins than the flat sheet?
options: Each fold stands on its edge, so it is hard to bend
check.why: Each fold stands on its edge, so it is hard to bend. Picking 'more paper' misses that it is the same sheet. The coins are the same coins.

flow.do: Read the usual solutions and the creative ideas together. Then invent a new shape.
flow.say: Here's what engineers usually do, and some creative ideas. Can you invent something better?
flow.kid: Look at the usual ways and the creative ideas. Now invent your own. Can you beat them?
flow.think: Why can a rolled-up newspaper stand up on its own, when a flat sheet flops over?

challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. You make one sheet of paper hold as many coins as possible over a gap, by changing its shape.

challenges.title: Save the Egg
challenges.problem: Drop a raw egg from 1 metre onto the floor without breaking it. You must protect it with things that squash, so the egg doesn't have to.
constraints: The egg goes inside a plastic bag, to keep any mess in.
Use only things from home, like paper, cloth, sponges, straws or a paper cup.
Your protector must fit inside a shoebox.
materials: raw eggs, each in a small plastic bag knotted shut (a zip-lock bag is easiest)
newspaper, cloth, sponges, straws, paper cups, rubber bands
an old sheet or newspaper on the floor
general: Wrap the egg in lots of crumpled paper or cloth, which squashes and slows the egg gently.
Put the egg in a cup stuffed with sponge.
Pack the egg tightly into a box with sponge or crumpled paper on every side.
creative: Build a cage of straws that bend and crumple on landing, like the crumple zone at the front of a car.
Hang the egg in the middle of a box on rubber bands, so it bounces instead of hitting.
Copy a bicycle helmet: a hard outside with soft foam inside.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own egg protector. Draw it, build it, and drop it. What will you change next time?

setup.art: A raw egg inside a zip-lock bag, wrapped in crumpled newspaper inside a paper cup.
setup.caption: 1. Put the egg in a bag. Build a protector around it.

setup.art: A child holding the protector beside a measuring tape at 1 metre above a sheet spread on the floor.
setup.caption: 2. Hold it 1 metre up. Let go.

setup.art: The protector opened on the sheet: crumpled paper squashed flat, and the egg still whole.
setup.caption: 3. Open it. Did the paper squash, and the egg survive?

flow.do: 1. Put one egg in a bag, with no protector. 2. Talk about what will happen if it drops 1 metre. Don't drop it.
flow.say: If the floor stops the egg suddenly, the force is big, and the shell cracks. How could we stop it more gently?
flow.kid: An egg falling on the floor stops very suddenly. Crack! How could you make it stop gently?
flow.context: This is the first step of Save the Egg. You design a protector so an egg can be dropped without breaking.

flow.do: Help your child build a protector from things at home. Remind them it must fit inside a shoebox.
flow.say: Something has to squash when it lands. If your protector squashes, the egg doesn't have to.
flow.kid: Build a protector. Something must squash when it lands, so the egg doesn't. Use paper, cloth or sponge.
flow.parent: The idea: soft things that squash make the egg stop over a longer distance. So the push on the egg is smaller. Cars have crumple zones at the front for the same reason. Helmets have foam inside.
