quiz.p: A girl bends a bamboo stick into a bow for a game. Which shape change is this?
quiz.why: The stick curves, so it is a bend. Picking 'squash' is close, because the inside of a bend is squashed. But the whole stick is bending.

quiz.p: Which of these is a stretch?
opts: Pulling a rubber band round a bundle of pencils
Pressing a ball of dough flat
quiz.why: Pulling outwards makes the band longer. That is a stretch. Pressing dough is a squash, and wringing a towel is a twist.

quiz.p: Which of these is brittle, so it breaks instead of bending?
quiz.why: Chalk snaps when you bend it. Picking the eraser means mixing up soft with brittle. The eraser bends and springs back.

quiz.p: Which of these stays squashed after you press it, so it has a plastic change?
quiz.why: Clay keeps its new shape. In science, that is a plastic change. A tennis ball and a sponge are elastic, so they spring back.

quiz.p: In the clay drop test, what should you change?
opts: The height and the size of the ball
quiz.why: A fair test changes only one thing. Picking 'height and size' means two things change at once, so you can't tell which one mattered.
quiz.context: In the clay drop test, you drop equal clay balls onto a plate from different heights, and measure the flat patch on each.

quiz.p: In your clay drop test, the 40 cm patch came out wider than the 80 cm patch. What is the best thing to do next?
opts: Repeat each drop three times and compare
Decide that height makes no difference
quiz.why: One odd result can be a fluke, for example a ball that was a little bigger. Repeating each drop shows the real pattern. Picking 'cross it out' hides a result you don't like, which is not fair science.
quiz.context: In the clay drop test, you drop equal clay balls onto a steel plate from different heights. Then you measure the flat patch on the bottom of each.

quiz.p: When you bend your finger, what happens to the skin on the back of your knuckle?
quiz.why: The outside of a bend is stretched, so the skin over the knuckle goes tight. The skin on the inside of the bend is squashed into wrinkles. Picking 'squashed' swaps the two sides.

quiz.p: A cardboard box has a wavy layer between two flat layers. Why?
opts: The waves stand on their edges, so the box is stiff but light
The waves make the box heavier
The waves are only there for decoration
quiz.why: Each wave is a little wall standing on its edge, so it is hard to bend. The paper is the same, but the shape makes it stronger. The waves do not add weight on purpose.

quiz.p: A fielder catches a cricket ball. What does the force from the hands do?
quiz.why: The hands push against the ball's movement and stop it. Picking 'speeds it up' means the push was thought to go the same way as the ball.

opts: Squashes for a moment, then springs back
quiz.why: The wet ball prints show the ball gets flatter in a bounce. Picking 'never changes shape' trusts our eyes, but the squash is too fast to see.
quiz.context: In the wet ball prints test, you drop a wet ball on paper and look at the wet circle.

quiz.p: A young tree is allowed to sway in the wind. Another is tied tightly to a stake. Which one grows a thicker trunk?
quiz.why: Trees grow thicker, stronger wood where the wind bends them. Picking 'the tree that is tied' sounds caring, but the tied tree has no bending to answer, so their trunk stays thin.

opts: India's plate pushed into Asia and folded the rock up
quiz.why: The push of two plates crumpled the rock, like a towel pushed against a wall. Picking 'volcano' is a sensible guess about mountains, but the Himalayas are folded rock.

opts: You run, jump and carry things
You lie still in bed for weeks
quiz.why: Bones reshape to match the pushes on them. Running and jumping push on them, so they grow stronger. Lying still for weeks makes bones weaker, like an astronaut's in space.

quiz.p: A steel wire is stretched a tiny bit. What happens to the atoms inside it?
opts: They are pulled a little further apart
quiz.why: Stretching pulls the atoms a little apart, and the bonds between them pull them back when you let go. Atoms do not grow or vanish when you stretch something.

quiz.p: Which of these do scientists still argue about?
opts: What glass really is, deep down
Whether clay squashes when you press it
quiz.why: Glass is hard like a solid, but its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's. Scientists still debate how to describe it. The other two anyone can test at home in a minute.

applications: Potters, bakers, goldsmiths, blacksmiths and sculptors all change shapes with forces.
Car crumple zones squash on purpose in a crash, so the people inside are pushed more gently.
Bicycle and cricket helmets have foam inside that squashes to protect the head.
Steel I-beams, bamboo scaffolding and bicycle frames use shapes that resist bending.
Wavy tin roof sheets and cardboard boxes are stiff because of their folds.
Ropes, coir mats and woven cloth are strong because of twisting and friction between threads.
Springs in mattresses, sofas, pens and weighing scales squash and spring back.
Tyres, balls and shoe soles squash and spring back with every bounce and step.
Glass-cutters scratch a line first, so the glass breaks exactly where they want.
Doctors and physiotherapists use exercise to make bones and muscles stronger.
Gardeners tie young trees loosely, so they can sway and grow strong trunks.
Engineers test bridges and buildings to see how much they bend before they are built.
Earthquake scientists measure how rocks slowly bend, to learn where they might snap.
LIGO and other detectors measure space itself being stretched by gravitational waves.
Sugarcane juice machines and oil presses squash and squeeze out juice and oil.

open_questions.q: What is glass, really? Is it a solid, a very slow liquid, or something else?
open_questions.why_open: Its atoms are jumbled like a liquid's but stuck like a solid's. Scientists still argue about why it goes stiff as it cools.

open_questions.q: Can we predict exactly when and where something will break?
open_questions.why_open: Cracks start at tiny flaws that are hard to find, and they spread in complicated ways. Engineers add big safety margins because of this.
Rock bends slowly for years, then snaps. Scientists can say where earthquakes are likely, but not the day they will happen.

open_questions.q: How exactly do living cells feel being squashed and stretched?
open_questions.why_open: In 2010, Ardem Patapoutian's team found tiny gates in cells, called Piezo channels, that open when the cell is stretched. He shared a Nobel Prize in 2021. How bones use this to decide where to grow is still being worked out.

open_questions.q: How squashed can matter get? What is inside a neutron star?
open_questions.why_open: Neutron stars are squashed harder than anything we can make on Earth. Scientists don't agree on exactly what their centres are made of.

open_questions.q: Could we make materials that heal themselves, like bone does?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have made some self-healing plastics and concretes, but none come close to how well bone repairs itself.

open_questions.q: Do living root bridges grow thicker exactly where people walk?
open_questions.why_open: Trees grow thicker where they are bent. But nobody has carefully measured this on the root bridges of Meghalaya yet.

open_questions.q: Could gravitational waves tell us what happened just after the universe began?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists hope ripples in space from the very early universe might still be passing through us. Nobody has detected ripples from that early time yet.

maths.problem: In the paper bridge challenge, a flat sheet held 1 coin. A folded fan held 25 coins. Each coin weighs about 4 grams. How much more weight did the fan hold than the flat sheet?
maths.explain: The fan held 25 coins and the flat sheet held 1. 25 take away 1 is 24 more coins. Each coin is 4 grams. 24 × 4 = 96. So the fan held 96 grams more. Check: 20 × 4 = 80, and 4 × 4 = 16. 80 + 16 = 96.
maths.context: This is about the paper bridge challenge. One sheet of paper must hold as many coins as possible over a gap between two books.

maths.problem: The plate India sits on moves north about 5 cm every year. How far does it move in 20 years? Give your answer in centimetres and in metres.
maths.explain: Each year adds 5 cm. 20 lots of 5 cm is 5 × 20 = 100 cm. 100 cm make 1 metre. The real speed is about 4 to 5 cm a year. We used 5 to make the sum easier.
maths.context: Remember Make Mountains, where you pushed a towel against a wall until it folded? The real push comes from the plate India sits on, moving north into Asia.

maths.problem: You twist a lined paper strip. You turn one end a quarter turn, then another quarter turn, then another. How much have you turned it altogether?
maths.answer: Three quarters of a full turn.
maths.explain: Each quarter turn is one quarter of a full turn. 1 quarter + 1 quarter + 1 quarter = 3 quarters. One more quarter turn would make a full turn, all the way round.
maths.context: This is about the twisting activity. You hold a paper strip with lines across it and twist one end, and the lines turn into spirals.

roots.context: We have been learning how forces squash, stretch, bend and turn things. Now we ask what this tells us about hard things, and about touching.

deep_truth.truth: A ball dropped on wet paper leaves a print much bigger than its resting dot. It squashed flat on the floor, then sprang back up. The floor squashed too, far too little to see. So every bounce changes the shape of both things, even a stone floor.
deep_truth.habit: We sort things into soft ones that change shape and hard ones that don't. But every material gives a little when pushed. Hard and soft differ only in how much they give.
deep_truth.evidence: In the wet ball prints test, the bounce left a wet circle much bigger than the resting dot, so the ball squashed to push off the floor. A laser dot bounced off a mirror on a table moves when you press the table, so the table bends too.

three.who_am_i: Your bones grow stronger where they are pushed every day. Your body is shaped by the forces on it.
three.what_is_life: Trees that sway in the wind grow thicker trunks. Living things respond to pushes and pulls by growing stronger where they feel them.
three.what_is_this_world: Mountains fold and the spinning Earth bulges. Even the hardest rock changes shape when it is pushed.

roots.thread: When you press a table, your thumb squashes a little, and so does the table. The push comes from both of them changing shape together. It is always shared: the table pushes your thumb exactly as hard as your thumb pushes the table. So nothing can touch without being touched back, and changed a little. So things are less separate than they look. Each thing is partly shaped by everything that presses on it.

teachings.teaching: A living plant is soft and bendy. A dead one is dry and snaps. So the stiff and hard break, and the soft and bending last.
teachings.link: In this unit, a bamboo bends in the wind and springs back, but a dry stick or a papad snaps. Things that can give a little under a force often last longer than things that cannot.

teachings.teaching: You cannot step into the same river twice, because new water is always flowing past.
teachings.link: A steel table, a mountain and your bones all change shape under every push, mostly too slowly or too little to see. Heraclitus saw change even in things that look fixed.

science.text: A thing changes shape because its atoms are pushed closer together or pulled further apart.
When two things push on each other, the two pushes are always equal and opposite. Isaac Newton wrote this down in 1687 as his third law of motion.

other_view.view: A thumb and a table push on each other, but they stay two separate things. Squashing and pushing back are simply what atoms do. Calling it a sign that things are less separate adds nothing the physics needs.

how_we_found_out.context: Do moving things need a push to keep moving? This card tells how people found out.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, and later Isaac Newton, an English scientist
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: A moving thing needs a push all the time to keep moving. Stop pushing, and it stops by itself.
how_we_found_out.story: For nearly 2,000 years, many people followed the ideas of Aristotle, a Greek thinker. He taught that a moving thing needs a push all the time to keep moving. Stop pushing a cart, and it stops. So stopping seemed natural, and only moving seemed to need a force. In Italy, in the early 1600s, Galileo Galilei rolled balls down sloping wooden tracks. He saw that a ball rolling down one slope rolls up a second slope to nearly the same height. When he made the second slope less steep, the ball rolled further to reach that height. So Galileo asked: what if the second track were flat? The ball would never reach its starting height, so it would keep rolling. He said a rolling ball slows down only because of friction and the air. He wrote this in a book in 1638. In 1687, Isaac Newton made it his first law of motion. A moving thing keeps going at the same speed in a straight line, unless a force acts on it. So a force is needed to change how a thing moves, not to keep it moving.
